Rather than paying higher fees at tax preparation sites, I've used TurboTax for the past 15 years. Our situation is slightly atypical in that we do claim a minor tax credit for hosting an exchange student, but it's merely a matter of researching the correct form and you'll find it in TurboTax accordingly. They also facilitate importing wage/earning forms by utilizing your employer's ID along with your SSN to locate and extract the relevant data, saving you the hassle of having to manually enter it yourself.    Overall, it's a great low-cost tax preparation solution if you don't want to sift through stacks of paper and fill everything out by hand or pay higher fees at a tax preparation site. product_title: Corel Painter Essentials 5 For Mac And Windows
review_headline: Bitmaps only. Fun toy. But basically a teaser for Corel Painter.
review_body: PC-based graphic artists have been hit with two frustrations in recent years - Adobe's heinous new pricing scheme, and Microsoft's slightly less heinous reworking of MS Paint. I had high hopes that this program would help address the first issue. No such luck. But it's an awesome Paint program.  WRT Photoshop - the program claims Photoshop compatibility, and this is true, inasmuch as it can open .psd files. It even preserves layers. What it doesn't do is bring in anything path- or object-based -- no splines, no fills, no reshaping, no manipulations that aren't bitmap/pixel rendering. If you thought the price for this as a Photoshop replacement was too good to be true, you were right.  WRT Paint - this does everything you ever wanted from that toy. Layers (as mentioned above), a much less useless zoom feature, all sorts of fun brushes and effects (with stylus pressure support), pixel-based transforms, and even a better-designed color mixer. Sweet.  Once I stopped expecting too much from it, the program was a lot of fun to play with, with a few annoyances. First annoyance -- the help function takes you to the help files for Painter itself, not Essentials. So, you will read about this cool feature, and then, at the bottom of the page, be presented with an apologetic "Some features described in the Help are available only in Corel Painter 2015, and are not included in Painter Essentials 5. For more information about Corel Painter 2015, visit http://www.painterartist.com/"  (which is a store link). Essentials is the teaser for the more expensive program (which does support paths), and Corel makes no attempt to hide this. Second, as with all Corel's graphics programs, this software can only be installed once. Were you planning on changing machines any time soon?  Well, unless the first machine fails catastrophically, you can't take this with you.  Given the relatively low price of this package, I would still recommend it to budding artists and fingerpainting kidsof all ages. It's not a professional tool, however, and doesn't really claim to be.  (Note - if you're looking for a real artist tool in this price range, check out Autodesk's Sketchbook Pro. That has a much steeper learning curve, and is still bitmap-based, but does a much better job of emulating a real drawing board workflow.)

review_headline: one of which seems like a bug
review_body:
I used this software to file this year's tax return, and I discovered a couple of quirks, one of which seems like a bug. I imported last year's TurboTax return into the H&R Block program, and it seemed to import fine. I scrolled to the W-2 section, and sure enough it had my name and my wife's name listed. However, when I clicked "Edit" to see what information it had found, there was no salary information listed for either one of us. I figured this was because my company had not released it's W-2 forms for online download yet. So a few days later I went back to the W-2 section and clicked "import W-2". This time it imported the financial information, but it did so by creating two new records for my wife and me (there were now two records for me, and two for my wife). I deleted the old original records which contained no salary information, but in doing so I ended up with my wife's W-2 listed first, and mine second.

At this point I began completing the rest of my return and everything seemed to go fine until I got to the end of the Income section. At that point it told me that I had contributed too much to my 401K, which I knew was untrue. Upon closer examination, I discovered that the H&R Block program had added my wife's 401K contributions to mine and was treating it as one contribution for one person. I suspect it was doing the same thing for our incomes and tax withholding also because the current refund amount it was showing seemed very high compared to previous years. I rechecked all the boxes in the previous sections of the return, but found nothing that was wrong. On a hunch, I returned to the W-2 section and deleted my wife's W-2 (listed first) and then reimported it so that it appeared second on the list. Sure enough, it fixed the problem with the return telling me I had contributed too much to my 401K, and it then changed the current tax refund amount to the correct amount. I don't see how this could be anything other than a bug in the software. Hopefully this bug would have revealed itself somewhere down the line in the return process if I had not had a 401K contribution to alert me to a problem, but it's kind of unnerving to think this kind of bug can exist for something which could happen so easily (reversing the order of our W-2's).

Other than the confusion about how to import the W-2 information into the return, and the bug that I found, the H&R Block Deluxe return was easy to use and went well.

product_title: DeLorme US Software BU-353S4 with Street Atlas USA 2015 Plus
review_body:
If you’re after the short, down and dirty version, here it is…
This program is a complete waste of time and energy.

Now, for the actual review.

If you’re after a simple GPS or mapping program, others are freely available. And this program is about as far from “simple” as any software I’ve ever written, reviewed, tested, or even seen. It’s “EZ Nav Route Wizard” is their sad attempt at providing a simpler interface by bypassing most of their "features", but it’s power is nil. If you want simple directions from one place to another, that’s their way of giving it to you. However, I’m baffled by why, if that’s what you’re after, you’re even considering this. What DeLorme should have done, instead of wasting time developing a goofy simplistic option like this and sticking it in their ridiculously bulky and inefficient program is spend some time and effort simplifying the entire thing. Imagine the control panel/dashboard of a 777 jetliner, with a seemingly infinite array of stuff, and a button in the middle that says “Fly to Chicago”. Yeah, nice idea DeLorme. Why not just make the thing easier to fly? See, the bottom line is none of us is trying to fly a jetliner, we’re just trying to drive to a few places as quickly, easily and efficiently as possible, and we don’t need the dash of a 777 to do it.

If, like many people who were abandoned by Microsoft when they stopped producing Streets & Trips even though it was consistently rated #1, you’re looking for a program that serves as a GPS and a routing program, DELORME STREET ATLAS IS NOT IT. This program has extremely limited power in this regard – so much so that there’s no way to include it in that category. If you, for instance, have a round trip to plan, where you know your start and end points, and have multiple stops to make but aren’t sure what order to put them in, or lets say you’re a service technician or salesman or a delivery person and you’re trying to maximize your efficiency by adjusting your start and stop times for each day, along with the duration of each of your stops, throwing sticks to the wind and trying to make sense of where they land might be more productive than using DeLorme SA. It allows for NO start or stop time, and entering a duration for each stop is enough to make you want to hurt people. As a comparison, in MS S&T, if you want to adjust your start time or a stop’s duration, you simply double click that address in the left pane, which lies in the same window as the place where you entered it. Up pops the time window for that stop. If you want to do it in DeLorme SA, here are the steps… make sure you’re in the Route tab. Then click the Advanced button on the bottom left. Then locate (scroll if necessary) the stop you’d like to adjust and click on it in the center pane. Then click the Stop Pref’s button on the right side. NOW you can enter a duration for your stop. It makes me imagine a microwave where the some of the number buttons are on the left of the microwave, some are in the middle below the door, and the rest of the buttons are on the right side, and they seem to have forgotten to put a "start" button on the thing. And for good measure, let’s remove all the quick setting buttons from the microwave. You know, the quick minute button and all those – they’re way too useful.

My bottom line for this software is you’re probably only looking at it for one of a few reasons, and it just doesn’t do a good job at ANY of them. You’re options for a Streets and Trips replacement are thin for sure, and I’m still looking. If that’s what you’re in search of, good luck, SA is NOT IT. If you need a simple GPS/mapping program, this is NOT IT. Simple isn’t apparently in this software team’s vocabulary. And if you’re looking for a routing program of any kind, with any level of efficiency to it atall, this is also NOT IT.

This is, hands down, the single worst-written piece of software I’ve laid my eyes on since the Windows 3.x days. I wish 0 stars was an option. No joke.all, this is also NOT IT.

review_headline: Unassuming but Powerful (5th draft of this review – 21 February 2016)
review_body: In writing this review, please understand I have not seriously used any other software for writing screenplays than Final Draft (FD). To date, I've written six screenplays. My impression is how easy it has been to write them in FD. The creative process is difficult and the revisions seemingly endless and certainly laborious, but the actual writing in FD is smooth and cool. All its power is hidden: what you see in front of you are your words on a white screen. But underneath is a fantastic formatting engine, which indents action, parentheticals and dialogue according to Hollywood-accepted standard. My understanding is that all screenwriting software do this, but for me FD does it so well – and even takes a few intelligent guesses at your intentions – that I've never thought seriously to try other software.  As a screenwriter who lives in Australia but who enters screenplays in American contests, I love how FD easily converts A4 to US letter and then to PDF.  What I also appreciate are macros, which I'm not aware other dedicated screenwriting software have. Though the Macro module is rather dated in look and feel, it's wonderfully powerful. It allows me to easily (without coding) create auto-correct and auto-complete functionality. Eg, I can have FD automatically correct "sitted" to "seated" or better still when I type "its" I can make FD show me in a bubble "it's" to remind me writing "its" for "it's" is a common error for me as is "your" for "you're". One could say the Macro module makes FD stand out from the rest (assuming "the rest" don't have such a module). However, the module currently does have a bug: it essentially has to be launched then closed by clicking the OK button – the Cancel button won't do the trick – at the start of each writing session before the macros properly execute.  At the top of my wish list for the upcoming FD 10 would be the ability to create a flowchart so that a story can be planned in a more visual manner (at the moment I use Scapple for this). I would also love to see a character template instead of the current Character Navigator, which I find I rarely use.  I love FD and I give it five stars. Giving five stars does not mean FD is perfect but it's doing the job wonderfully.  To return to the beginning, I have not used other major screenwriting software so my recommendation for Final Draft is not meant as a disparagement of competing brands. I have seen video tutorials on some of the other big names and some of the lesser known ones and each has one, two or three features I wish Final Draft had. But it is my belief FD has more streamlining features than any one of the others. Therefore, it's my opinion that Final Draft has been engineered with a screenwriter's workflow in mind. It really works beautifully.

product_title: Her Interactive Nancy Drew: Sea of Darkness
review_body:
Because the previews for this game were terrific, it's safe to say that every Nancy Drew gamer couldn't wait to play it! But did it live up to the hype? I would say yes & no. This game didn't "wow me" like I thought it would. I will have to play it a second time to see if it's worthy of keeping.

The one strong positive about this game was the huge improvement in character development! Labyrinth of Lies and The Shattered Medallion suffered in this field (as have a number of other more recent games), & I'm glad that HerInteractive took the time to fix that for this installment. Every character in Sea of Darkness is distinct, each with a story that unfolds as the game unfolds. Even pets play a part! Nancy's story is deepened as well, which makes the game feel progressive.

Other pros include:
-Good soundtrack (while it could have been better, it's much improved over the last few games, so I listed it as a pro)
-Variety of places to go, & items to get
-Good graphics in every part of the game
-The plot was for the most part, realistic

One thing that I didn't like was how the puzzles were done. Aside from the music box, the triangle puzzle box, & the word search code, the puzzles were focused too much on numbers, &/or were just remakes of puzzles from older games. And because most of them were over-complicated & didn't connect with the story well, they slowed down the action of the game, which took away from the fun of it. I also didn't like how the hotel bar's kitchen was done. I mean, serving food was another puzzle! It would have been much more interesting to actually make/serve Icelandic dishes!

Furthermore, it bothered me how much the game had in common with Danger on Deception Island, one of the great older games. But that just might be me being picky, since I love that game, & I like each game to be unique...

Overall, I would recommend this game. While it's not as as great as I hoped it would be, I do think it is a step in the right direction, and I think it has something for old and new fans alike. Feel free to see my other reviews for my favorite games!

***UPDATE: I have since played Sea of Darkness a second time. It's not a game that I'm going to love and keep playing over & over (for the reasons above, and the fact that it was even less fun the second time around). So I've decided not to keep it. I do still stand by my review, it is an improvement for HerInteractive. But Danger on Deception Island is soooo much better, you all should check it out!***nk it has something for old and new fans alike. review_headline: Photoshop Elements 12 heads and shoulders above Corel's Paint Shop Pro
review_body:
I am an amateur photographer and may not be a computer expert, but no slouch either when it comes to being a reasonably competent user of computers, software, etc. I had a version of Corel Paint Shop Pro Photo X2 Ultimate purchased four years ago. I have hated that program from the very start, found it unintuitive, complicated, and absolutely frustrating.... Looking up how to do things like HDR corrections, panorama compositions from multiple images, etc. never worked like the tutorials, menu options were not even close to what I had, etc So I was researching new editing software for a while. And while PSE 12 seemed to be the type of software that was designed for my needs, I was very apprehensive of the many, many negative reviews... Seemed like LOTS of people had problems with (a) download crashes, and (b) horrible experiences with Adobe support via chats. For these reasons I hesitated and tried to live with Paint Shop Pro, blaming myself for not being savvy enough to use the software properly....

Finally last night I had enough with Paint Shop Pro, it just plain sucks... I read many reviews of "what's the best photo editor out there" and can't for the life of me understand the users that had nice things to say about Paint Shop Pro and claimed it was a viable alternative to Photoshop. Either they are paid endorsers or just masochistic super-nerds who get off working on esoteric computer gibberish programs. Anyway, not for me, thank you very much. I became so frustrated I finally uninstalled the Corel garbage and felt immediately happier, lighter somehow... So much so that I decided to gamble on the PSE12. Went on amazon.com, boldly clicked on Download, crossed my fingers, and waited for the dreaded download/install problems to start, steeling myself for a couple of hours of chatting with some clueless CSR in India. Well, guess what??? No problems whatsoever. None. Downloaded, installed, and started running smooth as anything. Andtalk about intuitive. In no time I was able to do things like the aforementioned panoramas beautifully, simply, and without having to decode Corel's myriad of inexplicable icons and clattered UI, not to mention their tiny fonts.

I can't address the customer service horrors others have reported with Adobe customer support, as I haven't had reason to seek help yet. Nor did I have any of the many reported download/installation issues others have been reporting. I am not saying others are wrong, there is way too much smoke for there to be no fire, so to speak, but I simply did not experience anything of the sort. Thanks to PSE12 it's almost like I have found new enthusiasm for photography, I haven't caught myself even once today nostalgically thinking of the good ol' days of film and cursing digital photography for having been invented. Buy this program and discover how much fun it is to do digital editing again.

review_headline: Solid Norton update - but doesn't retain any remaining Norton360 subscription, and the install trashed one Windows 8.1 computer
review_body:
Norton Security with Backup is the latest version of Symantec's trusted cross-platform security and utility suite (formerly known as Norton 360 Premier). This new release adds some solid features not present in its prior incarnation known as Norton 360 Premier, including support for 10 devices (Windows, Mac, Android), Identify Safe password management, an updated / simplified user interface, and the Norton Virus Protection Promise (which provides remote support for virus removal at no charge if the automatic engine can't remove an infection).

And while I like the new features and the increased flexibility beyond the "1-3 PCs" offered in the prior Norton 360, my initial experience left a bad taste.

First of all, even though this is essentially the latest version of Norton360 Premier, the install does NOT retain any prior subscription you may have. So unless you REALLY need the new features in this release or need to support more than 3 devices, wait until your existing Norton 360 subscription is near its end before upgrading to Norton Security.

Secondly - and more concerning - is the stability of the installer. The first machine I tried to install this on was running the latest version of Windows 8.1 (with all latest Microsoft updates). The installer recognized a prior installation of Norton 360 Premier and proceeded to uninstall and reboot to continue. But on restart, Windows indicated it was attempting an "Automatic Repair". Ultimately, the Windows repairs FAILED - the error (0xC000021A) is a corruption of the Windows login files that could not be fixed by Automatic Repair, or even attempting to boot into Safe Mode. Lucky for me, I had a recent image backup of this Windows 8.1 install, although I suspect I could have tried to reinstall Windows 8 from the USB media.

Speaking of Backups - once again, the Backup capabilities of Norton Security are very basic and file-based, ultimately tied to Norton's online backup services. You get 25GB of free storage but there is no ability to perform a Windows system backup like TrueImage and others offer (Norton used to offer Ghost but this capability has long since been removed from the suite). So while your files are protected, your system is not.

Some may be surprised to see there is no CD or physical media - you are pointed to a URL (website) to enter your key and download the Norton setup program (a 1MB file), which you then launch for an additional (125MB) download of the actual product installer. Given that fewer devices are bundled with CD/DVD drives, I think this is a better approach - it always gives you the latest version of the installer and allows Norton to stay up-to-date with platform changes.backup services. Also the three month subscription to Ancestry.com was a nice bonus. It seems that most of windows feature has been included into this version. You can go to their website to see what isn't included. Probably the biggest problem with FTM is problems with the GEDCOM format. GEDCOM is the de facto standard for genealogical data. Every genealogy app should not only support it, but have no problems with it. For FTM, an application that has been developed since 1989, a application that is self touted as being "the #1 selling family history software", you should be able to have a handle on the most standard file format out there. It is disappointing that this issue plagues this software. Two star loss as importing data from reunion wasn't as smooth as it should have been.

Overall though this is a very good product, there are other options out there. One option is to just use the Ancestry website (Amazon won't let me put the web address in this review). While it might cost a little more, they have a lot more data.

I have a small company. That means I have a mailing list that includes names numbering in the tens of thousands. Of necessity, I've used Excel for quite a while. It's undoubtedly a powerful program and is probably able to do many of the things I'd like to do. But to say that Excel is obtuse would be understating it. I tried using Numbers, but found it unstable with a database this size. I dug through Excel at some length, trying to learn what I needed to learn. But as with many things Microsoft, you'd need to take a course or purchase a wheelbarrow full of books, and that just rubs me the wrong way (especially since I've spent decades as a programmer). In the end, I've ended up writing my own programs to manipulate the data in the ways I needed.

Then along comes FileMaker. It's been around for ages, but I never thought to try it before. In just a few hours of playing around, I had it doing most of the things I could never do in Excel. I could view and arrange data in meaningful ways that will allow me to glean more useful information from my customer data. Sure, I looked at the Filemaker tutorials (meager) and at the Filemaker Forum (most helpful). But I'd spend hours digging through Excel sites and never managed to do more than basic stuff with it.

I've found that it's quite a simple matter to update my database files from csv files (normally the way I receive much of my data). There are many ways to massage the data before bringing it in. I can also easily export csv (as well as many other formats) for other external processing. I should also say that it's quite fast--faster than Excel for what I'm doing. Sorts are completed almost as soon as they're begun. It's also been quite stable during the time I've been testing.

It's not perfect. When exporting to csv, Filemaker won't let you export column headers as the first row of text. That's an oversight that needs correcting, since it's a very common practice in csv. You can still do it in a roundabout way by exporting to Excel and then saving as csv. But I'm looking forward to forgetting where Excel is on my computer. There are a few operations that are less-intuitive than they might be. But--unlike Excel--I could find my way through these issues quickly.

There are many aspects of Filemaker that I won't be able to try until my company grows. review_headline: It's no substitute for typing, but pretty accurate and useful
review_body:
I was once the ghostwriter on a book whose author supplied me with a batch of pages, all of which he had dictated using Dragon, the speech recognition software. Those pages were a mess, filled with misspellings and other errors. \\"Would\\" became \\"wood\\" and \\"is\\" became \\"as,\\" and so on. An interpreter would have been helpful. I came away from the experience with a negative view of this software.

Now that I've used it myself (with a complimentary edition courtesy of the Amazon Vine Program), I realize that the results are dependent on the quality of the dictation. Speak clearly, making sure to emphasize the words so they cannot be mistaken for their homophone, and it works very well. It won't give you any writing skills you don't already have, and I wouldn't recommend using Dragon as a replacement for a pen or keyboard. If, like me, you're interested in typing up a lot of handwritten material but are overwhelmed at the thought, this is excellent.

The results are not going to be perfect, but perfection is rarely possible when typing either. Dragon does not eliminate the need to proofread your work. A guide is included with what to say if you need an exclamation point (\\"exclamation point\\"), a period (\\"dot/point/period/full stop\\"), 5'3\\" (\\"five feet three inches\\"), and other potentially tricky commands.

A microphone is provided, a \\"Stereo Communication Headset\\" it's called, with two audio jacks and an attachment for computers that can only accommodate one jack.

Be sure you are aware of the system requirements before attempting to install the software. I tried it out on my 11-year-old Dell laptop without success. It did install without difficulty on my new Asus laptop.

Brian W. Fairbanks

review_headline: Not worth buying unless you have a new model camera

Adobe does hold its customers hostage to a remarkable degree even for software companies which are notorious for getting the laws rewritten to provide legal cover. If you have the latest camera and need the latest version of Adobe Camera RAW to convert your camera's RAW files to TIFF format then Lightroom 5 is your only choice with Adobe.

Lightroom 5 is not really a full release upgrade from Lightroom 4, only a way for Adobe to continue to have sales revenue coming in from this application. It is much the same with Photoshop CS where CS 4 provides 99% of the functionality and performance of CS5 and CS 6.

The only virtue of Adobe's Lightroom 5 is that you can still buy a DVD and install it onto your computer and only need an internet connection to activate the software and then to create a user account with Adobe (much more difficult than it should be) so you can download the latest bug fixes and patches to the software along with the current release of Adobe Camera RAW.

Lightroom provides a way to catalog and tag your files in a very crude kind of Digital Asset Management but it is designed for one user with one internal or attached hard drive and is very much a dead ended design. If DAM is what you need there are better products available that are better long term solutions and ones that work well with a network RAID set of hard drives (ReadyNAS, Synology, etc).

If all you want to do is tag your files there are alternative applications that are designed for this purpose and put the information into the EXIF file instead of sidecar files which is a more cumbersome and less robust approach though one that Adobe seems wedded to much as with Microsoft and its stupid registry and dll architecture. Both Adobe and Microsoft sacrifice performance and stability without a second thought if it locks in their customers and keeps out competitors.

review_headline: A GOOD OLD SOUL TRYING TO LEARN NEW TRICKS
review_body:
The original Fate was the PG version of DIABLO: cartoonish graphics, simplified quests, very limited gore and a cute child/hero running, fighting (and fishing!) in armor. The dungeons were endlessly random, the beasts well deserving their fate and the weapons and trinkets imaginative (and surprisingly expensive!). Overall, very fun to play!

Its first sequel, Fate: Undiscovered Realms, offered more of the same in a second set of dungeons. And the second sequel improves little beyond offering yet another set.

Very few things are new in this standalone incarnation. True, you can now choose amongst four races (Human, Shadow Elf, Half-Orc and Cogger). The best one is still Human, a true Jack-of-all-trades: Elves are agile but have a very hard time defending themselves; Orcs are clumsy tanks, strong but with low dexterity; whereas Coggers are strong geeks but with no magical abilities.
There are new armor sets, new weapons and spells and new pets. On the other hand, I could discern no change in the graphics and sounds compared to the previous installments.

Finally, the two previous dungeons each get twenty extra levels to explore and plunder. This is a steal because for the price I remember paying for the first game you now get both the original game and its first expansion. On the other hand, you may find exploring all three dungeons and completing one run-and-fetch quest after another a bit tedious. Nevertheless, it is still good casual fun.

RECOMMENDED.

review_headline: Not to be trusted as a company or as a technical product
review_body:
I purchased the Dreamsuite Bundle Photoshop Plugins from autoFx.com years ago for $399 and initially it worked fine.

Then I switched to a MAC computer from a Windows and so I download the MAC version which did not work and sat on my desk top for a further two years.

Eventually, I contacted the company about 5 times and was ignored for 4 weeks.
I was so frustrated with the lack of support and the money I felt I had lost to this company, that I wrote a blog post much along the same lines as this one.

About a week later the CEO emailed me explaining they had recently had a change of management and apologized for the lack of customer support.
He was very nice and did all he could to resolve my incompatibility issues and I was delighted to be able to once again use the software I paid for.

Some months later, my Operating System was upgraded which is a fairly common occurrence with any computer regardless of whether it's a Windows or a Mac computer.
Once again the plugin failed to work.

I wrote to the Auto FX customer/ technical support again but this time the reply was not so helpful.
In fact, I would go as far as to say the person who replied was quite rude and abrupt.

I was "reminded" of how much help I had already received previously and told I would have to pay a further $299 to upgrade my software in order for it to work on my computer as the version I owned and had paid $399 for was now considered "legacy" and was no longer supported by the company.

So, the bottom line is this; This plug in series would end up costing me $698 to work, the initial $399 and then a further $299 just to make it work again.
How many further 'upgrades' and associated hefty fees would I need to pay when my computers operating system was upgraded in the future?

I understand being charged for optional upgrades for software which has been improved or had added features applied to it, but I resent and refuse to pay hundreds of dollars just to be able to continue using software I have already paid hundreds of dollars for!

I made an assumption that the plugin would always work, that the $399 I paid to AutoFX.com gave me a license to use that software for as long as I needed it.
There certainly was no information or TOS explaining that I would need to pay further fees if the software became incompatible with my computers current operating system.

I own thousands of dollars worth of licensed plugins and graphic software on my computer and to date, have only encountered this issue with AutoFX.com
Do all graphic software companies do this? In my experience, that depends.

For example, I own Filter Forge 4 Professional, Perfect Photo Suite, Substance Designer, Bitmap2Material and others and yes, some of these companies do charge a small fee (Approx $80) when they add additional features to their software.
However, I can continue to use the older version and it continues to be supported technically by the company.

My Filter Forge is updated all the time as they fix bugs and improve performance and its done with no charge and the same applies to Perfect Photo Suite.
Both of which I owned when I was on Windows OS and moved to a MAC OS and neither company charged me to download a compatible version.

Personally, I think it's immoral to take hundreds of dollars from people for a piece of software and then demand almost the same amount again just to allow them to continue using what they had paid for, regardless of how long ago that was.
$399 is a lot of money by most peoples standards and as it happens for me, I had about 12 months use of that expensive plugin.
I have asked for a refund three times and each has been ignored.

This morning I downloaded the free demo of their DreamSuite plugin just to see whether it was worth paying the additionalfee to "upgrade"
It installed fine and shows in my Photoshop CS6 Filters list but nothing happens when I select it.

So in closing and based on my experience, AutoFX.com customer support is terrible, the software reliability is sketchy at best and the company ethics for paying customers is appalling.fee to "upgrade"

review_headline: Good, but lots of room for improvement.
review_body:
I have been using Family Tree Maker since it was made by Broderbund. I'm using this version on Windows 8.1. I had absolutely NO problems installing it, and the only bug I've noticed is it freezes if left running for a long time (as in days). As stand-alone software (without using Ancestry.com) it is acceptable for a beginner. It has decent documentation, online help, and a large online community, including a facebook page.
I would not recommend it to a beginner using it with Ancestry without explaining to them the horrible nature of online trees. Ancestry does not include documentation for sources that aren't on their site, so you have no way of knowing how accurate these trees are. Trees that have multiple, valid sources for each piece of information show the same as some guy who says "grampa's name was James Smith, and this guy's name is James Smith, so that must be grampa". I've seen mistakes repeated throughout multiple trees, where people just copied it from one to the other without verifying. These trees can make a good framework, a good starting point, for you to verify the information yourself, but to just pull it into your tree unchecked is to invite errors that will magnify the further back you go.
Ancestry provides a lot of excellent information that you can pull up with FTM with their search feature. United States Census information from 1790-1940, marriage data bases from several states, military records from most American conflicts, and cemetery and obituary records just to name a few. Their search is horrible, they seem to think the more names they provide you with the better off you'll be somehow, but this is rarely the case. A search for James Ronald Smith will provide you with every James Smith, Ronald Smith, and everyone with the initials J and R in their names (Thomas J. Smith, Thomas R. Smith, for instance). This wouldn't be so bad, but they put what their search engine thinks is most likely first, then all the mass of information terribly disorganized after. I usually find what I'm looking for buried in page 2 or 3. It also ignores locations and dates - a search for someone in South Carolina who died in 1800 will show results for Civil War records of someone in New Jersey. The only way to change this is to set items to exact matches, and that runs the chance of missing names that a census taker spelled a little differently, for example. They won't let you restrict the information to items from South Carolina, for instance. The LDS church site, Familysearch.org, lets you do this and it is a big improvement.
Despite what can be implied from some of their statements, you cannot access your tree from multiple machines. You can only sync your information with one machine. If I have my tree synced with my desktop, and I'm taking my laptop to the library, I have to manually copy the file from the desktop and put it on my laptop. This is pretty lazy for 2014. I'm not sure what the apps they mention will do, but looking at the descriptions, it''s pretty limited.
It's a stable system, it doesn't seem to crash with large numbers of entries, as some I've seen do. You can print your information in a variety of formats fairly easily. It is easy to use. Offline documentation is good, online documentation is not. Online user trees suck, online databases are great. Better search, and show all sources online and you're looking at a 4 or 5 star system.

It is a sweet deal for Microsoft - regular, steady, predictable income - but it is a bad deal for the customer if you don't want every upgrade.  At $47.99/year (as of this writing), it is a significant annual expense (even if some point out it is $4/month).  Equivalent apps (albeit with less functionality) can be had for $9, $19, or $29 with free upgrades for life.    Overall, it is a great product with a customer-hostile business model.  On the upside, business models can easily change and make this product overall a winner again. review_headline: Upgrade went fine - So far all works well
review_body:
After reading the reviews of all the issues with people having when upgrading, I was very concerned about doing the upgrade myself and then messing things up. So I took the careful approach, and all went fine.

Here is what I did:

1. Validate and repair your database file in the current version (under the File/File operations/validate and repair). This will check and fix most issues. Save the new verified file with a new name. Save that file also to a memory stick.

2. Install the new Quicken 2014 on a different PC than your primary one. (You can install up to 3 copies for personal use).

3. Download the mondo patch from Quicken support page and update 2014 to the latest version.

4. Then, copy your data file from the memory stick to the 2nd PC. Then import that file into Quicken 2014. If everything goes in fine, then you have proven the file import will work.

5. Next, install Quicken 2014 on your primary PC, do the mondo patch update there as well, then import the same file on the primary PC.

6. This also means you have a backup installation on your other PC as well. Make sure to backup regularly your data file and copy it on the backup PC.

Also, be sure to NOT use that backup or second PC for adding transactions - or syncing with the web and your accounts! Only use your primary computer for adding new transactions and syncing with Web and online accounts.

This method worked without a problem for me.

The new screens for linking to your online accounts work great and needed nothing to work when upgrading in my case from 2013 to 2014. Mobile works fine as well on my Android, but i only use that to check, and not to update with transactions.

Theres not a lot of new stuff from 2013, but if you have older versions, i would say you should upgrade just for the better online features. I have not had any issues come up so far, As far as I am concerned this is a good upgrade.

Video Capturing.

When video capturing you must understand codec formats. All capturing devices can be programmed to various formats. Formats most associated with DVD's are MPEG-1 and MPEG-2, and those associated with HD are MPEG-2, MPEG-4 Part 10, AVC, and newer. AVI and mp4 are only container files in which these multiple formats can be placed. These formats are highly compressed and requires very fast processors (cpu, gpu) to get good results in real time. If your computer can't keep up or are marred with errors then you have to use lesser compressed formats such as MJPEG that do not rely so much on the processors. The results, however, will be larger files and require much more disk space, especially with longer movies or surveillance situations. Even with fast systems, this is recommended because the resulted videos will be of higher quality. You can later recompress the videos to DVD's and HD/Bluray with even better quality than trying to do it in one shot. All formats can be adjusted during capturing or finalizing to achieve balanced results. Hope this helps.

review_headline: There Are Some Quirks, but This Is the Best Player I've Used Yet
review_body:
In fact, it's a bit looney to just call it a media \\"player\\", this thing does a lot, maybe too much which is why there are some quirks. OK, Pros & Cons:

PRO
-It plays my 4K video clips ABSOLUTELY SMOOTH, I can't believe it, first player to do so. QuickTime Pro runs like a train going uphill with square wheels when I throw 4K video at it. PowerDVD Ultra is smooth as glass, I didn't expect that (I'll list my PC specs at the bottom, that does come into play). SDtandard HD video even straight off of my 5D Mark III simply looks and plays great, and I'm pretty picky.
-Image Quality: they claim that videos look better when played back. I was skeptical; not now. They look great and PowerDVD does leverage custom profiles if you have a wide gamut monitor, which I do. And being H.264 compliant is a plus because there's more image data available to enhanced in that compressed format.
-The app just looks good. I know, seemingly insignificant attribute, but I like a good UX (user experience) and the default skin looks awesome.
-BluRay support: there are three components to play a BluRay disc due to the built-in digital rights management: 1)the player has to be able to handle the bandwidth, compatibility is not enough. PowerDVD does this extremely well. 2) your monitor must be HDCP compliant, and 3) your graphics card must be HDCP compliant. That means Dual Link DVI or HDMI ports. Otherwise not even PowerDVD can play the BluRay disc on your PC.
-Windows 8 ready! I'm now running Win8 Pro 64bit and have been hammering away at the user interface, trying to get it to crash, but PowerDVD has basically yawned at me. So far, very stable, even the added Mobile Sync Service it runs (see next line)
-OK, this is pretty cool: PowerDVD runs a small service in Windows that connects most mobile devices to the PC when on the same network. So I figured this meant that I download an app on my iPhone and it becomes a remote, and that's true. But they've added another feature that really isn't related to running videos: my iPhone becomes a trackpad using the PowerDVD app. Even if I quit PowerDVD it still functions as a trackpad on any app! You have to start PowerDVD to get it going but then can quit it later. Because of the high res screen on the iPhone (I'm sure Droid phones work equally as well), the trackpad is quite precise! The only caveat is I haven't figured out how to right-click.
-Last thing: Fast. Really fast. The software fires right up with no lag.

CONS
-The user interface's left-side navigation is somewhat confusing. They made it too cluttered and often you click on something that you think is the right thing and it turns out it isn't. I probably just need to get used to it.
-Importing assets: when you first fire up the software, it's defaulted to auto-import videos and pictures from your libraries... problem is, it is SLOWWWW. I applaud Cyberlink for attempting a way to give us Digital Asset Management, but to be honest I just want to right-click a video file and have it play, and play well, and THAT is what PowerDVD shines at.

I saw some other reviews where there were complaints that installing version 13 disables version 8. I won't make friends saying this, but why on earth would you want such an old version anyway? Algorithms and CODECS and integration with the latest operating systems have improved drastically in the last few years, I would ditch the old versions with glee. Just my $0.02...

I can't comment on Ultraviolet and 3D, I don't work with those formats or services. I did look up some reviews on PC Mag and others who claim that 3D is handled surprisingly well, but personally I don't know.

I'm psyched, I finally have a player for HD and 4K vid that looks awesome and runs like butter. Forget all of the other bells and whistles, that to me is worth the price of admission.

review_headline: Is it worth the switch from another PC security program? Eh...
review_body:
I've used both McAfee and Trend Micro anti-malware programs in the past, and decided to give Norton a try since my latest Trend Micro subscription was about to expire.

The first thing I noticed about Norton on the PC is that it tends to run in the background more than other programs. Whereas Trend Micro would be in your face with scan notices, monthly reports, backup requests, color-coded links in my Internet browser, and giant warning screens that websites may not be safe, the most I get out of Norton is a little notification telling me it did something (such as performing a backup while the computer was idle or that it blocked a popup because it potentially contained malware or there was a security certificate issue). For someone who's well-versed in using computers, they'll probably prefer Norton's less-intrusive MO, but I'll say this for Trend Micro - they really hammered home how important security is and encouraged you to take an active role. I could easily see someone not very good with computers just assuming Norton will protect them from everything no matter what they do.

I found Norton's online backup to be simple and easy to use - just select folders or files you want to back up and let the program do the rest - but was a little disappointed that selecting what I wanted backed up was about the only feature I had access to. For example, this product comes with 25GB of online backup, but as you're selecting files and folders it's not telling you how much space they are using or how much space you have left. Just as a test, I selected a folder I knew had over 25GB of content in it and attempted to back it up (in addition to the folders I was sure I was backing up) and Norton faithfully started the backup without ever checking if it could actually complete the task. From a programming standpoint, this is a very simple thing to implement and a clear oversight (and potentially devastating for those with Internet usage caps or slow upload speeds).

While I don't miss Trend Micro's habit of making web pages into a red, grey and green menagerie of links (FYI you cn turn that off in the TM settings), Norton's online security seems less robust to me - where TM would pop up warnings, Norton just lets the site load. In fact, Norton doesn't even stop most popups in my experience (it's caught one so far out of maybe ten) or catch most redirects (i.e. the link is supposed to go one place but takes you to another).

One thing that did impress me about Norton is the speed - where a TM or McAfee full scan would take an hour or more, Norton blew through in about 15 minutes. It also handles updates automatically so I don't have to check my definitions every few days (or authorize the program to check).

I've also installed this on my Android phone (a surprisingly painless experience thanks to a QR code). Backing up contacts was a snap, but that's about all I've had cause to use so far on it. I'm a bit concerned that my phone's Chrome caught a security certificate issue with a website before Norton did.

Overall, I'm impressed with Norton in some areas and disappointed by it in others. Don't get me wrong, it seems to be a capable program, but now that I've experienced this I don't see a compelling reason for people currently using other security programs to make the switch, provided they're satisfied with what they have.peeds).

Adobe Premiere Elements is one of the best selling consumer video editing software packages on the market. That title was well earned with earlier releases, but - in my opinion - one that the software failed to live up to in more recent versions due to bugs and other glitches. Using PE 12, I can honestly say most of those bugs seem to be gone for the Windows version, and all I am seeing is a great program I enjoy using.

So, what makes PE 12 so enjoyable to use? Simplicity and power. While the current version is not quite as user friendly as some of the earlier ones, most users will find it much easier to figure out than, say, Sony Vegas Movie Studio (my other favorite Windows video editing program). Adding special effects is easily done, and the various modes allow more experienced users to skip over guided creation when they are ready to do so. As well, PE 12 has seamlessly integrated DVD creation that will let you make professional-quality menus from templates with ease (add Photoshop Elements for the ability to completely customize these templates).

Please note that prospective buyers should consider the Premiere/Photoshop Elements software bundle that is also available. The bundle tends to provide significant savings over the combined cost of the two programs, and Photoshop Elements can be very useful when producing videos (creating DVD menu templates, making still images for the videos, etc..).

Rating: 4.5 Out of 5 Stars (rounded to 5). Powerful and easy to use video editing software. I can highly recommend the Windows version.

review_headline: Great for multi-tasking on a Mac and using Office 2013
review_body: Frustrated with Mac Office software that was last updated in 2011? Want to take advantage of all the great updates in Office 2013? This amazing software allows you to combine the convenience and great hardware of a Mac with the awesome features of all the latest updates to Windows 7 or 8 and Office 2013. I use this everyday at my law firm where I can switch easily from Mac OS to Windows Office using a four-finger swipe on my MacBook Pro. It amazes everyone who sees it how seamlessly Parallels allows you to take advantage of both operating systems. And because you can copy and paste from Mac to Windows, you can do all your research in Mac, and then do all your drafting in Windows. It gives the flexibility of essentially having a two monitor setup with only a single screen. The only caution is to make sure you allocate enough RAM and processing cores to Parallels in the settings menu to make sure that your programs run at full speed in both. I have allocated four cores to Parallels and 3GB of RAM, and have not noticed any slowing on either Mac or Windows with that setup. The single core that Parallels allocates by default is not enough. Also, I would recommend setting up Mac BootCamp and installing Windows with BootCamp before installing Parallels because it allows you to boot directly into Windows if you would like, but also Parallels can read the BootCamp partition and allow you to run both operating systems simultaneously. I really can't recommend this program enough, and it goes on sale frequently, you can find it for sometimes as little as $40.

I had used a much earlier version of Nero burning, back in the good old days of Windows XP, without any problems but having changed my computer to one running Windows 7 Pro I had to find a more modern version.

I purchased the download version of Nero 2014 as an upgrade from their trial version and immediately after installation started to experience difficulties with my computer, which is a high spec machine well in excess of the requirements specified for this package. Considering that there is no way of loading this software without using the serial number I consider this to be pretty poor customer relations. They did say that since this was a technical problem they would pass it on to the technical department for consideration, but I have had absolutely no response from them.

When dealing with other companies, on the very rare occasions that I have had software problems, there has never been a problem in getting a refund, even when the software has been on a physical disk which has had to be opened.

Having conducted this transaction through PayPal, I felt fairly confident that they would be able to help me out, however, I quickly discovered my error as they only deal in problems with physical goods and not downloads, so I am considerably out-of-pocket and feel pretty sore about it.

This company seems extremely good at bombarding one with emails telling of the delights of using their software, but when there is a problem they just seem to take the money and run. Sufficient to say that I willnever deal with this company again.

Freedom is the best part of this game, both in character development and in what you can do in the world. For example, there are at least 5 ways to get past a locked door. You can use lock picking skill, a magic spell, pickpocket the key from an NPC, follow an NPC inside once you know their schedule (if applicable), or destroy the door. If an NPC is around and you get caught doing any of these things, there are consequences. You're forced to decide what is important to you, and to live by those choices. You can choose to kill a shopkeeper and loot their inventory, if it serves your needs better than trading with them. You can help stop a bank robbery during the day, and then rob the bank yourself at night. There are no character classes, only the dichotomy of magick and technology. You can choose to rely on either one, or build a more neutral character that survives in other ways. You can start as a pure melee fighter, adding some thieving skills perhaps, and eventually become a master of persuasion with an army of followers. You can learn different types of magick or technologies, and there are many different possible followers who either complement or conflict with your character's choice of magick or technology. You can be a master of bows or throwing weapons, and choose a magickical or technological bow later on. You can also become a master of firearms, which is technological from the beginning. You decide how you make your way in the world. There are many side quests, with the main quest line always being there to fall back on when you feel like continuing.

The character models are sub-standard and overly generic, but manage to give your imagination enough to work with. The movement and combat animations are decent, and give life to the characters when they're not standing still. If you don't expect much from the graphics then you won't be disappointed. Most of the major characters have good voice acting, and the story and dialog will draw you into the game. Much of the dialog depends on your character, so playing different types of characters will allow you to experience the whole game.

Then I saw Anime Studio Pro 9 in a few YouTube tutorials, and it was on sale on Amazon, so figured I would take a chance on it. Well worth the $65!! I would have easily spent that just for the auto lip-sync feature alone! You just import an audio track, make a switch layer for your mouths, and setup the switch layer to use the audio track as its mouth reference. In seconds, you have your mouth movements done for you automatically! It has saved me soooo much time, and I am actually excited about animating my project now instead of manually agonizing over every little mouth movement!

The interface can be somewhat confusing, and it took a little getting used to. I am still trying to master the art of bone rigging. Make sure you do all your character and scene setup on FRAME 0! I constantly forget to do that :-/ Luckily there are so many tutorials on the SmithMicro site and YouTube to get you started. Overall, I'm really impressed and having a blast using it. There are a few bugs here and there, and some rare crashes and occasional odd behavior. But if it does crash, at least it has an auto recover feature that usually brings you right back to where you left off. Register and Update to 9.2 from the web site as soon as you install. That fixed a few bugs for me.

The Library feature is great. Love being able to setup characters and scenes, and whenever I need them again, I just import them from the library. Saves a lot of steps. Also you can record common actions like walking or blinking, and reference those in your main timeline to reuse over and over. It has a pseudo 3D environment that makes scenes look very realistic, as well as some physics elements I haven't really played with yet. I'm still trying to master the layers and depth-of-field options. You can import 3D objects and scenes from other programs like Blender and Poser, or create simple objects within Anime Studio. I could go on and on, but suffice it to say, I really like the software and would recommend it! :-) It helps if you already have some knowledge of programs like Photoshop & Illustrator, video editing or other keyframe animation sofware, but if in doubt, just watch some of the tutorials on YouTube to get a feel for whether or not it would be a good option for your needs.

Also, I would highly recommend purchasing a Wacom tablet! It makes drawing the vector points and shapes much easier. You can do it with the mouse, but the tablet is more natural.

ѾѾ The previous X4 version introduced the HDR (High Dynamic Range) \\"Exposure Merge\\" tool that is Corel's foray into HDR software, which Adobe and other graphics software vendors are also incorporating into their tools. HDR processing involves combining multiple exposures of the exact same shot (which is easier if your camera has an Automatic Exposure Bracketing (AEB) function) to create a high dynamic range photo which can display a higher tonal range than what the camera is capable of capturing in a single exposure. There are various software specifically dedicated to HDR processing. For the past five years, since version 3 in 2008, I have been using the excellent [[ASIN:B002CIP12U Photomatix Pro 4]] software for HDR processing. This X5 version of \\"Exposure Merge\\" adds new black-and-white HDR controls and a very useful \\"Preview Alignment\\" option to visually inspect the positioning of your merged photos. There is also a new \\"single RAW photo\\" option where you can create an HDR photo using a single RAW image by defining an \\"EV Interval\\" to simulate a triple-bracketed shot, and the software will then split the single RAW image into three exposures before combining them together. This single-shot-HDR option is also offered by both \\"Photomatix\\" and \\"DxO Optics Pro\\" software.

On a relative scale specifically rating its HDR functions, I would rate Photomatix 5 fuzzy stars while this PSP X5's HDR \\"Exposure Merge\\" tool only gets 3.5 fuzzy stars rating. This X5 \\"Exposure Merge\\" is improved over the X4 version, which I would rate at 3.0 stars. But both Corel and Adobe still have a long way to catch up with the powerful and flexible offerings in Photomatix. In particular, I found the \\"Exposure Merge\\" tool in PSP to be lacking in its ability to precisely align bracketed photos and thoroughly and flexibly remove ghosting artifacts, which is something that Photomatix does a very good job at. If you use a tripod-mounted camera to shoot bracketed photos where nothing in the scene moves the least bit, then the \\"Exposure Merge\\" tool consistently outputs good HDR results. But when shooting portraits or landscapes, or shooting hand-held, bracketed photos often have misaligned objects and/or moving objects in the shots. Even bracketed portrait shots of a person using a tripod can result in tiny movements by the person that require excellent alignment and deghosting by HDR software, and Photomatix currently beats PSP's \\"Exposure Merge\\" tool in this area. PSP's \\"Exposure Merge\\" tool frequently has ghosting artifacts leftover either from movement of the camera by the photographer or movement of objects in the scene. This ghosting is especially evident in scenes such as landscapes where various plants may be moving in the breeze or portraits where the subject has slightly moved in between each bracketed shot. Photomatix also includes a plethora of other tone mapping, image stacking, and on-the-fly editing adjustments, including being able to define specific areas of photos to deghost and specific areas of photos where I can use the original image instead of the HDR output. I use these Photomatix functions a lot because I always aim for very natural-looking HDR images, instead of the surreal psychedelic HDR images that are, all too often, output by people. HDR software can be abused to create unnatural over-saturated photos that become tiresome to look at. Using Photomatix on an image of people set against a beautiful background landscape, I can tell the software to use an original un-HDR'ed exposure of a photo for the people's faces while letting the software HDR-process the rest of the landscape, and this is very useful to me because HDR-processed skin tones can sometimes look unnatural. PSP's \\"Exposure Merge\\" tool cannot perform these functions that I described. So a good HDR workflow would be to HDR-process your bracketed photos first using Photomatix, and then further edit the HDR output in PSP, perhaps performing some sharpening as the last step before saving the files.

ѾѾѾ While the \\"Manage\\" and \\"Adjust\\" tabs are more simpler, clean, and organized in their user interface layouts, the \\"Edit\\" tab feels very busy and crowded, and it can be hard to find tools, especially when you are initially familiarizing yourself with all ofthe software's dozens of tools. One ambiguous example is that under the 'Adjust' main menu option of the \\"Edit\\" tab, there is a 'Brightness and Contrast' option that then opens up a submenu containing the 'Fill Light/Clarity' tool. But the 'Adjust' menu also lists a similar tool called 'Fill Flash'. At a minimum, the 'Fill Flash' tool also needs to be moved into the submenu below the 'Brightness and Contrast' option. Ideally, both 'Fill Flash', which has 'Strength' and 'Saturation' slider settings, and 'Fill Light/Clarity', which has 'Fill Light' and 'Clarity' slider settings, should be combined into a single tool window containing three or four sliders, instead of confusing users as to which of these two tools to use.

ѾѾ The software links to a variety of searchable online help and built-in tutorials. As with some of their other recent software releases, including the previous PSP X4, Corel has the help documentation in this PSP X5 set up so that clicking on the 'Help' option from the menu and then selecting 'Help Topics' starts up your browser and takes you to Corel's Web site where all of the help topics are accessible online and can also be searched. I really wished that Corel gave the user the option, during the initial software CD installation process, to either install the entire help documentation locally on the computer or to link the software to Corel's online Web site. After all, being dependent upon online access in order to access help information can be problematic if the user needs to search the 'Help Topics' from a place where there is no Internet access. On October 2 2012, Corel released a 76-MB 'PSPX5_LocalHelp.exe' patch that does install all of the help files locally on the computer, but after I installed this patch, clicking the 'Help Topics' still always brings up my browser and opens up a new Web page to display Corel's online help content. And there does not seem to be a way to configure PSP X5 to default to offline mode and use the locally-installed help files even when no Internet connection is available. But you can still manually access the locally-installed help files by directly pointing your browser at the directory path where all of the help files are installed. The main Web page for the help files is located in the directory path below:

32-bit C:\Program Files\Corel\Corel PaintShop Pro X5\Languages\EN\Help\wwhelp\wwhimpl\js\html\wwhelp.htm
64-bit: C:\Program Files (x86)\Corel\Corel PaintShop Pro X5\Languages\EN\Help\wwhelp\wwhimpl\js\html\wwhelp.htm

If your PSP install also constantly redirects you to Corel's Web site after installing the help files locally, you can point your Web browser to this location to access the locally-installed help files. This locally-installed help documentation page, complete with a search function, works well using either Internet Explorer or Safari browsers, but Firefox just displays a blank two-framed page.

Ѿ My one main gripe about this and all previous versions of PSP is that it still does not have a tool for stitching together panoramic photos. Photoshop has the \\"Photomerge\\" utility and Canon has \\"PhotoStitch\\" for creating panorama photos. But PaintShop Pro and also Corel's Photo-Paint in their Graphics Suite package have been missing this very useful functionality for a long time. Corel really needs to add a panorama merge/stitch function to their ever-increasing rich set of tools. The current way to create a panoramic photo in PSP is an entirelymanual and laborious process. You first create a new canvas that is large enough to hold all of the expected overlapping photos, you then copy each photo into a separate layer, decrease the opacity of one layer so you can see through it while you manually move the layer around to visually align the edges of one photo with the overlapping portion of another photo, and you repeat this tedious process for all overlapping photos that will be used in the panorama before setting the layers' opacities back to 100%. Needless to say, this is both time-consuming and highly prone to error, and the manually merged result only works if you shot the overlapping photos using a tripod with a panning head and a very level camera. By comparison, Canon's \\"PhotoStitch\\" program is very user-friendly and flexible with its options, and it automatically aligns and merges photos in the order that you specify.

During almost one year of weekly usage before writing this review, I have had the software crash or hang about 3 or 4 times total, and this includes running the software on an old underpowered Windows Vista laptop and a tiny Windows 7 Dell Mini 10 netbook. The previous X4 version used about 900 MB of disk space, and version X3 required 3GB of disk space, which tells me that prior to X4, PSP had become very bloated and disorganized. By comparison, Adobe's Photoshop Elements 11 requires a whopping 3GB to 4GB of disk space, even though it has less features and effects than PSP.

௫ Fuzzy Wuzzy's Conclusion:

For overall bang-for-the-buck combination of very affordable value and feature-packed power in a commercial photo-editing software package, this PSP X5 currently reigns supreme, beating out Adobe Photoshop Elements 11 and all other photo-editing software that I can think of. If you want something even less expensive, look into a freeware graphics software called \\"GIMP\\" which offers a ton of graphics editing power for free. And if you have no experience with graphics software or if you do not want to spend time learning its complexities, look into the free and easy-to-use software called \\"Paint.NET\\".

Despite the significant performance improvements in versions X4 and X5 (they are roughly 50% to 100% faster than X3 and also far more stable), it still does have its slow areas of laggardly performance. In particular, this is not a good software for processing RAW files, both dueto its slow RAW converter and due to its limited RAW compatibility.

If you want the deluxe photo management and editing solution, deluxe in capability, cost, and complexity, using Adobe's Lightroom and Photoshop CS are the way to go. Otherwise, this PSP X5 is an excellent \\"Photoshop for the masses\\" alternative. If you primarily shoot in RAW, adding Corel's AfterShot Pro allows for great RAW handling followed by photo editing in PSP X5. And if Corel's HDR feature in PSP X5 has whetted your appetite for HDR processing, you should seriously consider getting Photomatix Pro (currently at version 4) since its capabilities exceed anything that Corel or Adobe has to offer.

If you are using a version of PaintShop Pro prior to X4, is this PSP X5 worth the upgrade?

Most definitely! There were many dozens of improvements in going from X3 to X4. Even if you ignore all of its new features and enhancements, just the fact that X4 and X5 run a lot faster and are more stable than X3 is a compelling enough reason to upgrade. However, the improvements in going from X4 to X5 are more incremental; there were far more improvements in going from X3 to X4. But with a good discounted price, it is still worthy upgrading from X4 to X5.

If you are just starting out with photo-editing, should you buy this PSP X5 or Adobe Photoshop Elements 11?

I feel that PSP X5 is a far more capable and feature-rich program than Adobe Photoshop Elements 11. PSP X5 is more like the full-blown Photoshop CS version than APE11. APE11 includes more built-in layer styles that PSP X5 does not have, although if you are just starting out, you will not miss this. Once you become proficient in PSP X5, you can create your own styles and record them as scripts to repeatedly reuse. Photoshop Elements has a much larger user base than PSP, and there are numerous sites to download brushes and textures from, but it is easy to convert Photoshop brushes to use in PSP, so that is not really a problem. APE11 has more adjustment brushes than PSP X5 when it comes to brushing on effects like dodge, burn, and saturation. But PSP X5 has more artistic tools than APE11, useful for painting, drawing, scrapbooking, and graphic design, and PSP X5 is more useful and flexible for manipulating images other than photos than APE11. PSP X5 requires less than one third the disk space to install than APE11, and at the time of this review's writing, Amazon has it priced lower than APE11, even though PSP X5 is far more packed with features. But... if you think that you will eventually migrate up to Photoshop CS, which is far more complex, powerful, and expensive, then starting out with APE11 will give you skills that are more transferable to Photoshop CS than becoming proficient with PSP X5.
