review_body: I use to use this product when I took computer classes when I was younger, and it helped me then. To this day, it STILL helps me. So, regardless of age, this program is worth every penny.

Love this Quicken software. I was using Quicken 2011 and upgraded to 2013. For all intents and purposes the program seems nearly identical for the functions I use. I use the program to keep track of bank accounts, my business, and my financial investments. The main reason for upgrading, is that I like to have the ability to continue to download stock prices on a daily basis. Quicken has gotten to the point where it is so sophisticated that there is really little new functionality to add. The main addition that I can see, is the ability to sync to IOS (Ipad, Iphone) and Android apps. That's great, but I doubt I'll be using that function because I don't like to have my financial information on a cell phone which can be lost or stolen so easily. But for many people I suppose this will be a major improvement. For the rest of us, the main reason to keep upgrading is really for a reason analogous to \\"subscription\\" software...that is the ability to do online banking, and downloading stock prices on a every three year renewal basis.

I first started using Quicken in the early 1990s when it was much less sophisticated, but was very easy to use. Over the years they cluttered the software so much that I switched to Microsoft Money. I used that program for years and preferred it to Quicken of that era. But when Microsoft abandoned Money, I returned to Quicken...version 2011. Much to my surprise, Quicken had improved dramatically to the versions they were putting out in the late 90s, and around 2000. The software became less cluttered, more responsive and returned to the ease of use that Quicken had been so famous for. The conversion function that Quicken inserted for those switching from Money was extremely impressive. It converted everything I could imagine accurately and completely. Bravo to Intuit, because as we know very often \\"conversions\\" leave us underwhelmed and disappointed.

My initial take on Version 2013, is that it is just a teeny bit slower than 2011...just a tad less responsive. But it is certainly in the range of acceptability, and the functionality is first rate. I especially like the versatility of the financial investment parts of the program.

Finally, I am able to easily run the accounting for my law office practice. The software keeps track of revenues and expenses, and allows me to use subcategories for each which really helps around tax time. I am able to prepare very helpful and complete reports to easily insert information into my tax returns...this is in addition to the data that I can automatically transfer into Tax Cut or Turbo Tax. You can even generate reports that match the specific Tax Return forms. So overall the program is very flexible, comprehensive, and allows you to input and output information in a variety of ways...leaving you to decide which way you prefer to do it. Well Done.

Always easy to follow Turbo Tax. I am looking forward to downloading directly from my brokerage (whenever they are ready)

review_headline: Five stars for the program, 0 stars for customer service...
review_body: I'm pretty much a novice when it comes to antivirus programs - I have small experience with McAfee (which I found clunky and irritating) - but after our last computer crashed and burned (from lack of antivirus software...), a friend recommended Kaspersky.  I've used Kaspersky 2009 (with an immediate upgrade to 2010), and now 2012, and have been very happy with both, with very few exceptions.     I like the expandable desktop icon on Windows 7 - part of the overall sleek, simple design that I find very pleasing.  Kaspersky 2012 is even simpler in design than 2011, which was nice.  I appreciate an antivirus software that doesn't blink and flash all over the place - yet you can get much more detail quite easily.  So it's user-friendly and simple, but allows more advanced users (this does not include me) to see the finer points of their antivirus software operation.  The \\"safe-mode\\" for website navigation is a great feature - since I sometimes find myself in the position of having to do sensitive things (online banking, for example) on a public network, I appreciate the extra layer of security.  It's also nice to have the \\"safe-mode\\" for the computer as a whole - I've had a few computers bogged down with viruses or other problems in the past, and I would've liked to have a \\"safe-mode\\" for retrieving pictures from the dying harddrive...  I find the website pop-up warnings unobtrusive enough - and I've used Kaspersky long enough now that most of the sites I frequent that raised a flag have already been added to a \\"safe\\" list.  Kaspersky's pretty sensitive to inappropriate material - I think a page on knitting tripped a warning about drugs (hemp fiber) - but I don't find it annoying or inconvenient to click a button to add a site to the safe list.  I appreciate the frequent updates of their database - this hasn't slowed down my computer or interfered with other programs running (actually, it usually updates without my knowledge), and it's comforting to know that they update their database so frequently.    Now for the negative - customer service is lacking, in my experience.  I installed Kaspersky Internet Security 2012 on a computer that already had about a year left on a license for Kaspersky Internet Security 2010, and initially had a little trouble getting the license to appear with the correct term.  I sent off an e-mail to customer service about this... and never heard back.  I quickly realized I just needed to plug in the security key that came with the 2012 software, but I would still have appreciated a response from customer service.  In the past I also had trouble with customer service when I renewed my license for Kaspersky.  I purchased two years of coverage following the link in the program itself - only to find a 20% discount advertised on the homepage.  I immediately wrote customer service asking if I could receive the discount, since my order was placed only moments before finding about the discount, and since I was a returning customer.  Customer service wrote me back with an apparently automatically generated e-mail asking if I had received my confirmation e-mail, and stating that if the e-mail did not resolve my problem, to reply with more information (order number, mailing address, etc) and they would get back to me.  I replied with the requested information, restated my question... and never heard back.  This was just over two years ago.    Also, although it's just a minor annoyance:  I renewed Kaspersky for two years, and after one year began receiving multiple e-mails urging me to renew my license or it would expire in x number of days.  I checked my license length on the program itself, and it was fine, so I ignored the e-mails.  I've had no problem with continuation of coverage, but the e-mails were a little confusing and annoying.  I've used Kaspersky since August 2010 and have experienced no virus or internet security issues in that time - the interface, security, and ease of use make Kaspersky worth it tome despite the dismal customer service.
This program has gotten rid of so many of the problems that I struggled with using a multi-year outdated program.

review_headline: I Do Not Like Green Eggs and (Sage) Spam
review_body:
At my small engineering firm we have used Peachtree (now part of Sage) since 1985. After the original purchase we purchased only four upgrades, the last being Peachtree 2012.

We have no problems or unfulfilled accounting needs and do not want Sage 50, Accounting 2013. Nevertheless, we have received at least fifteen letters, emails, and phone calls that are almost threatening in nature with their warnings of bad things that can happen without another upgrade. A Sage \\"Final Notice\\" means nothing, the Sage sales spam continues. Sage, do you have no traditional values of customer service and honesty?

Accounting is not an area of rapid development, there is no need for an annual product cycle.

Peachtree Accounting has a proud history since 1975. Wiki says, \\"Peachtree was the first business software introduced for microcomputers and the oldest microcomputer computer program for business in current use, with the possible exception of the original Microsoft Basic interpreters, also introduced in 1975.\\"

I was surprised by the number of sharply negative reviews. If it were not for the aggressive, less than honest sales spam and the cost of each year's (unneeded) new edition, I would give the product four stars. We found the online payment option buggy and stopped using it after a two-week trial but otherwise get along fine running the 2012 version. Sage product support is too costly; but we get along fine for our infrequent questions with a couple of inexpensive third-party books.

I guess we will end up before too long with QuickBooks. QuickBooks was not around when we bought our first Peachtree license in 1985 but has long since surpassed Peachtree/Sage in market share for small business accounting. When we interviewed eight candidates to replace our retired bookkeeper, everyone preferred QuickBooks to Peachtree. Our CPA firm also prefers QuickBooks.

review_headline: Not sure if I like it or not...
review_body:
I'll start this review saying that I never owned a Win 7 PC, so I went from Vista to 8. This means I wasn't inducted into the whole pinning programs to the Taskbar thing as defined in Windows 7; I knew that feature as creating a quick launch shortcut and I never really used it as I feel it clutters the taskbar with crap. I also need to add that I run three monitors, which is a very important detail as far as Win 8 usability goes. Win 8 has certain features that improves multi-monitor support, but certain use paradigms makes it the worst version of Windows for multiple monitors that I've used.

With that said, Windows 8 felt extremely alien at first. Sure, it's still Windows and has many familiar things, but the lack of a Start Menu entry in the taskbar is quite a problem. I suddenly find myself extremely reliant on the Windows key in the keyboard. Windows 8 also has some odd choices with panels that come up when you place the mouse in the upper right and upper left regions of your monitor, a task that is very difficult to manage with multiple monitors as the mouse will simply hover over to the next screen rather than trigger the panel. I ended up using the Microsoft Keyboard and Mouse Center (I own an MS keyboard) to map some of the keyboard's custom keys for calling the Charms Menu (it's the one that comes up when you hover on the upper right corner of the screen and has functions for searching, settings, and others depending on the app - think of pressing the settings key on an Android device).

One other big change that I can't really handle well is the change of the desktop from the old work environment to an application that holds the old work environment. For instance, in older versions of Windows, pressing the Windows key + D would show the Desktop on its own. Doing the same now will show whatever app is running on top of the Desktop. Then there's the whole full screen app concept (MS used to call these the Metro apps). They're a pain if you're using a desktop or laptop without touchscreens. Basically there are no buttons to minimize, maximize, or close these apps. In a tablet you swipe from the top of the screen to the bottom to close these apps. Seems easy enough. With a mouse, you need to move the cursor to the top of the screen, where it turns into a hand. Now you need to hold the left mouse button and drag down. However, there is only a visual cue when you hold it as the app turns smaller and the screen is full of the background color. As you drag down though there is no further visual feedback until you're past the lower half of the screen, so for about 50% of the screen real estate it doesn't seem like there's anything going on with the app and you can't close it. Took me a few days to realize this details. Now these apps don't take up too much RAM, but the end result in the meantime is that once more, the Windows key suddenly becomes as important on a PC as the Home button is on an Android or iOS device. I don't really care for that change at all.

Another big change is when the Start Screen comes up; it initially seems to hide the \\"All Programs\\" section of the older Windows Start menu. In order to unveil those you need to right click and a bar at the bottom opens up with an option labeled \\"All Apps.\\" Click on that option and now you get to see all the programs in your PC. I notice what MS is doing is increasing the use of the right mouse button in many areas where it wasn't necessary before. Interestingly, for all these details to make it more usable and friendly in certain areas such as tablet use, the OS still has really odd needs of staying with old conventions. For instance, I installed it on a PC I built from scratch and Win 8 never gave me any help in finding the Storage Volumes applet for initializing my addition hard disk drives. Coupled with the lack of an \\"All Programs\\" entry in the Start Screen as it's hidden by need of a right click and no \\"Run\\" box in it, I was wondering if the OS even detected the additional hard drives! Then I realized you don't need a \\"Run\\" box as you can just type in the Start Screen. Still, another thing that was really intuitive (you had a box you could type in) was replaced by a hidden feature. That seems like the norm in Windows 8.

Let's talk about multi-monitor support: what's good and what needs work. First of all, Windows gains the option to run the Desktop task bar across all present monitors and you can customize it so that all the taskbars show the same info or only info for software running in that particular screen. Bravo! Windows really needed this added. Unfortunately, triggering all those odd corners is now extremely unreliable. Start Screen? Better hit that Windows key in your keyboard. Charms panel? Windows Key + C is now your best bet. Cycling through apps (the top left hotspot)? Windows Key + Tab. So it's one step forward in multiple monitors and a few back, though in all honesty, those steps back hurt not just multi-monitor use, but desktop use in general (and laptops without touchscreens).

So enough about the changes. Windows 8 is really fast, looks pretty, and seems to be way more compatible with older software than Vista was when I initially used it. I haven't really run into any serious Windows 8 compatibility issues so far. MS needs to work better on the relationship between the Desktop and the Full Screen environments. It's very jarring. MS also needs to make all those hidden panels and features more intuitive; they seem to be banking on users getting used to them and then not think about it, but for the moment they introduced an odd learning curve and they did so at a time when more and more people are considering alternate operating systems. Will they accept Windows 8's learning curve or will they take this as the chance to buy their first Mac or run their first Linux box?

At the end of the day, Windows 8 is a capable Operating System boasting powerful compatibility with older versions of the Windows OS. Unfortunately, some of the changes that MS chose make little to no sense and introduce a lot of usability conflicts. In the end though, it's still Windows, and it's much cheaper than older versions so that helps a bit...

The overhauled UI three years ago was bold and refreshing; now it is as boring as a Toyota Camry (but highly functional, so it is not necessarily a bad thing).  You still get nagging prompts to log on to your Norton account (so that Symantec can peddle additional products to you), and there is still no way to cut off the internet traffic without going through a complicated menu.      During the full system scan, the computer noticeably slowed down (i7 quad processor with 8 gb or RAM), which was surprising.  I did not encounter any slowdown issues with the previous Norton versions of the past 3 years.    Those little problems aside, Norton is still a top performer.  Integrates very nicely into Windows 7 SP1.  Has been trouble-free so far.  The manufacturer says that all the detection algorithms have been improved, and I take them at their word.    Overall, I recommend Norton Internet Security 2012 provided you can get it at the right price.

review_headline: Excellent for dictation; a big time saver; very accurate
review_body: Before purchasing Dragon NaturallySpeaking I evaluated Windows speech recognition. The Windows capability seemed quite poor. It made many errors, and even though the words appeared inside its dictation box, they magically disappeared when I inserted the text into a document. So, Windows speech recognition was very unsatisfactory.    I'm using Dragon with my own Sennheiser headset. While the training is optional during setup, I chose to do it. The accuracy seems incredibly high. My initial use was to transcribe handwritten notes from during some telephone interviews into Microsoft Word. It's a big timesaver, even though I am still in the learning mode.    I had an unusual experience which further reinforced how accurate Dragon NaturallySpeaking is. I was doing a particular dictation session and the accuracy seems quite low at least relative to previous experiences. Still, however, the accuracy was better than Windows speech recognition. Offhand I estimate during this period the accuracy was perhaps in the 90 to 95% range. Then, I realized that I was wearing the wrong headset! I was still wearing the headset that I use with my telephone. The Sennheiser headset was laying on my desk about a foot in front of me. So even though I wasn't wearing the correct headset Dragon still was performing a lot better than Windows speech recognition. Of course, when I put the headset back on, full accuracy returned.    Another benefit of Dragon NaturallySpeaking is that it has quite useful on-screen help and help menus and a user manual that is available in PDF form.    Yes, I dictated this review.    So far I am very happy with Dragon NaturallySpeaking and I highly recommend it. Definitely worth the investment compared to Windows speech recognition in my view.

review_body: This will be brief. We have several Mac Pro 8-Core towers and had intended on using Drive Genius 3 for what should have been simple, routine maintenance and tune-ups.    Although as a California based business we make every effort to support other California businesses we are chagrined to say we cannot support Prosoft or its Drive Genius 3 product with a favorable review. It's not that it is a bad product. It is simply that, for $100 ($84 - Amazon?) and what it offers (or DOESN'T offer) it is not a good value. From a business perspective, that implies not much confidence in a company's product or services).    BOTTOM LINE: SAVE YOUR HARD EARNED $100 (oops, again!  $84). Apple offers standard tools (Disk Utility, Tech Tool Pro, even start up from OS 10.6.3 disk to repair permissions, etc) to address any issues. The only thing that we added was Super Duper (now THAT IS an undervalued product - certainly WELL worth more than what it's developer, ShirtPocket, sells it for!). I'm quite hung up on this point!

review_headline: Some good features but SO crashy!
review_body: I bought this software to take notes in law school.  I've used several older versions of MS Word on Windows at work for years, so not having to learn new software was a big factor in my choice.  The other major factor was that it has audio recording integrated in it.  That is a really nice feature because it creates reference points as you type so that it is easy to go right to a particular point and get any words or phrases that you might have missed in class.  Now the bad stuff.  It crashes all the time.  I keep both my OS and the Word software updated but so far that hasn't fixed the problem.  Switching between views makes it crash about 80% of the time, literally.  Knowing that I save then switch views, let it crash and then reopen Word and the document.  Documents also become easily corrupted and I've had to copy and paste the body of a document to a new one to fix that.  Another problem which is not a bug but, in my opinion bad design is that the audio recording is only available in \\"notebook\\" view, which is a simplified view with very limited access to other features.  So say you're humming along taking notes in class and want to insert some smart art (like a hierarchical flowchart, which is great for things like UCC codes or jurisdiction).  You have to switch to draft or print layout view, and then back to notebook, and... CRASH.  Bummer.  The last point I have is really just preference.  I liked the older, I think pre-2007 versions' layout of menus and features.  I thought they were more I intuitive and straightforward.  My recommendation: If you want to record while notetaking this is a good program.  If you don't need audio, go with an earlier version if you can find it, or run bootcamp and run a windows version.  If you don't need audio and you're relatively new to MSWord, save your money and get NeoOffice or another flavor of OpenOffice for free, but don't forget to donate to the good people who keep it going.  :)

review_headline: Like other Adobe products, I found this one baffling too
review_body: I have lately been looking for a photo editing program with more advanced edit functions than I have with ACDSee Pro. It would be nice to have an organizer built in, but that's not necessary if I'm using the program for straight editing.     I have already tried Photoshop Lightroom and found it had some tools I want, but it was extremely hard to find files and handle the \\"Library\\" and it didn't read all of the files in each Windows folder. So today another attractive offer came for Photoshop Elements and Premiere. I decided to try that one out too.     The interface was a bit more usable than Lightroom, but only a bit. It has an organizer and you still have to import files into it rather than reading them directly from a Windows folder view. As in Lightroom, I find that whole process unnecessarily time consuming.     However, the worst thing in this program is a very simple detail: When you first view files in the organizer you cannot see the FILE NAME of the image you've selected. Not anywhere on the whole screen. You have to right click and look at the properties of the file. If you've named your files to have a distinct identity and number for each one, as part of the work flow, this omission is a big time waster. I finally figured out that in the View menu there is a setting \\"Show File Names\\". I checked this, but nothing at all happened. I was frustrated until I finally gave up on this and moved on to file editing. Then suddenly, a newly imported file had a filename on its thumbnail. Apparently in order to change what you see in the thumbnails you have to delete them from the Organizer and import them all over again. Another time waster. The question in my mind is, why did the program come with a default setting NOT to show file names? Strange.     Aside from this, let's talk about the tools. There is a glamorous video showing how you can snatch people and other unwanted objects out of the picture with one click of a mouse and the space they occupied is miraculously filled in with detail that you couldn't see in the original photo. Could this be true? The program can make up details? Upon searching for this miracle, I realized that it is an everyday clone tool or healing brush. The videos are a little misleading because the area filled in was obviously \\"cloned\\" from another image of the same scene sans the people. Therefore it takes a bit of forethought to pull off this off as shown in the video. The healing brush is very ordinary and many photo edit programs have it. As for the other tools, I haven't tried them all, but the one that corrects lens distortion did not work well. I took a file that I had corrected in a few minutes with ACDSee Pro and could not do the same thing with Elements, even though the two programs list at about the same price.     I had ordered Photoshop Elements 9 and Premiere Elements 9 together, thinking that Premiere was an integrated add-on which provided more functions. review_headline: A wonderful, simple, and possibly addicting game
review_body: This review is for the Steam version--I do not know if the retail requires activation.  This review will be done in a different format than my other game reviews.  Scores in each section are out of 5.0 stars.  My apologies for the length; I can't seem to write short reviews.    Torchlight is a new entry into the Diablo-style hack'n'slash genre of games.  While it may seem derivitave, it bears mentioning that some of the team behind this game also worked on the actual Diablo games, and one of them is the guy behind Fate.    Customization (3.5):    Not much here to start with--three class archetypes to choose from (melee, ranged, or mage).  Each character has their own brief backstory.  I played as the melee class; my wife is playing as the ranged class, which involves both bows and guns.  More customization comes in upgrading your character--each one has three different skill tracks to upgrade.  Personally, though, I would argue that this game's REAL customization potential is in the loot.  This game is loot-heavy.  Some items have slots that you can upgrade with runes.  In town, there is an enchanter (which as another reviewer mentioned is the real money-sink in this game), and also an NPC who can combine duplicate runes into better ones.  Some loot is in \\"sets\\" that provide bonuses the more pieces you have equipped, though I've found mish-mashing stuff I find to be the best way to go.      Graphics (3.5):    Colorful.  Vivid.  Confusing.  The enemies will swarm you (load up on AoE skills!) and it can often be hard to tell exactly what's going on, but a few clicks of said AoE skill can usually clear them out fairly easily.  For those playing on non-gaming netbooks, there is a \\"Netbook\\" option under settings that makes it much more playable (we tried this with the demo on my wife's computer before I bought it on mine, and it seems to work well).    Pet (3):    The pet is an interesting mechanic.  The fish you can find throughout the game (via, well, an easy-to-graspfishing mini-game) can be fed to your pet for temporary transformations or stat boosts.  These will greatly increase your pets HP, and bestow temporary abilities depending upon the type of fish consumed.  They generally last for 120 seconds, though there are variations.  Perhaps the most useful aspect is the ability of the pet to run to town and sell stuff in its inventory, which is just as big as yours.  Due to the decently high drop rate of potions, the only thing that really might make you go back to town in the middle of a dungeon is using up identify scrolls.  You CAN learn an ID spell, though it takes up one of your 4 spell slots.    Gameplay (3):    The real measure of a game.  The gameplay here is not deep, thoughtful, or difficult.  The enemies--even most bosses--are pretty easy to kill.  This is not a criticism per se--I downloaded the demo before purchasing this game, so I knew exactly what to expect.  When it comes to games, I'll play a certain game for weeks on end, tire of it for a while, then play something else in a different genre.  This is a simple game, but the dungeons go on for a VERY long time.  I played through and \\"beat\\" the story (which ends on about level 35-40, I can't recall exactly).  I'm playing other things now, but I still bring this game up when I want some mindless loot-grinding.  It's a good game to kill some time while waiting for my wife to get ready if we're going out (she feels the same away about when I'm getting ready!).  Even though the main quest is completed, there are still NPCs outside of a secondary, more difficult dungeon (the Shadow Vault) that are giving me quests.    Bug, Glitches, Issues:    A relatively common one I've found is enemies and the loot they drop getting stuck in walls or behind objects that appear transversable but are not.  To my knowledge, no patch has been released addressing this, though if I am mistaken, please let me know.  Occasionally your pet will get stuck and trail behind you, though this is easily fixed by doubling back and running in a little circle usually (though it is rather annoying).  The save mechanic uses (in the Steam version, and when connected) the Steam Cloud.  HOWEVER:  The game does NOT require an internet conenction to play, or save.  I've found the best thing to do when done a session is open a town portal, and go into town.  The game saves, will reload you into town the next time you open it, and your portal back into the dungeon will remain there.  I've had several game-killing crashes (which on reloading means I start at the beginning of a dungeon floor), though this is not prevalent enough to make the game unplayable.    All in all, for a game that had a development-to-market cycle of 11 months, with an engine built from the ground up in this time, Torchlight is still surprsingly well-done.  The cost--$20 (I got mine for $10...a week later it was $5 in the holiday sale!  Oh well)--seems reasonable (if not, wait for another sale, it's sure to come!).  This game can definitely cause the \\"just one more turn!\\" (or dungeon level, or boss, in this case) mentality, but it is also easy to pick up and play for an hour without having to invest much thought or effort in it.  If you liked Diablo, Fate, or just the dungeon crawling, loot-grinding genre in general, this game is a can't-miss.    3.5 / 5 Stars Total (I wish Amazon allowed 1/2-stars).

review_headline: Easy-to-use, Intuitive, Reasonably-priced Music Notation Application
review_body: A little over 2 years ago, as part of the resurrection of my long-dormant music career after retiring, we bought a Yamaha music work station, as a way to play any music I would write or arrange.  At the same time, I began giving my wife lessons on the soprano recorder.  I was about to get my old stockpile of music paper out of the attic, but my wife suggested that there must be notation software that would make my life a lot easier.  At that time, I test-drove 4 different freeware products, selected the best-of-the-breed, and started to capture arrangements I had written many years ago.  Also, I began to create exercises, songs and recorder duets for my wife and me.  Unfortunately, the freeware product was not very robust and it kept crashing on me, as I frequently asked a little too much of it.    Due to this lack of robustness in the freeware, I continued my research for a better product.  I ran across a thread in a Yamaha forum, suggesting that Notation Composer from Notation Software, Inc. was a very powerful, easy-to-use music notation application.  The thread also noted that Composer compared very favorably in capability, and very importantly, in price, to the high-end products.    I have been using Notation Composer for about a year-and-a-half, and have captured most of my scores from my younger days.  Composer is a extremely robust application, and has very effective recovery routines (rarely needed), unlike the freeware I used.  The scores I have captured with Composer range from the duets that I've written recently, to dance band septet, swing/jazz band, concert band and full orchestra.  The product is quite intuitive, and the Help function is extremely well-written and detailed.  And, very importantly, the ongoing Notation Software Support has been fantastic, which is important to new users.  Also, the Forum subscribers have been very helpful.    I can play the Composer files on my PC, as I'm writing them, and they sound very good, even though I do not have a high-end sound card.  Also, my wife frequently plays along with Composer while she is practicing.  This gives her valuable reinforcement on keeping proper tempo.    The printing capability of Composer is excellent, with clear, sharp printout of parts.    Composer can also read midi files, and create scores that you can read and study, as help in writing your own music.    My wife knew very little about written music before she started to play recorder.  She likes to say that the only thing she knew how to play was the radio.  As her recorder lessons progressed, she received a number of song books for reading/playing.  Some of the songs were out of range for her instrument, so I gave her rudimentary data entry lessons on Composer.  She can now enter these songs into Composer, transpose them to any key that suits the recorder, and then print them out for her ever-expanding personal music book.  She very quickly picked up the data entry skills necessary to do this -- a strong point for the ease-of-use of Composer.    The Notation forums contain a wealth of information about user-written music and a lot of help in learning how to use Composer.  Sample a number of the shared items in the extensive \\"Share Your Music\\" Forum.  There is a broad spectrum of music written by Composer users.  Go to their home site and follow the forum links for more information.    In summary, Composer is a very easy-to-use, intuitive, reasonably-priced music notation application suitable to both beginners and experienced music lovers.  I highly recommend it.

review_headline: Perfect to learn first words and phrases, but no grammar
review_body: The software provides a nice start if you want to learn spanish, but it does not deliver a complete course up to a certain level. The set up is that you start talking about business and technology pretty quick, without having received any grammar and practice that comes with that. You learn words and basis phrases first, but only in the present tense.Past tenses or other tenses are not being explained, which is in my opinion more important than talking business (if I would go and talk business in spanish, I would like to know how to make proper phrases in general, before I can actually worry about business talk).  The word practice and the games are really good and very easy to use. It is also sort of \\"fun\\" so it does motivate a lot to do it.  The phrases however are a bit slow and a bit confusing, the words are first spoken in English and even I who does not speak any spanish (yet) can notice that the translations are not very accurate (which is in my opinion a very important thing in a language course). Since they don't explain anything else, about the grammar, it is a bit confusing when the phrases are not very correct. For example, the English voice says; What soup do you have? The spanish translation to that is: \\"Tiene sopa?\\" which I think means: Do you have soup? and has nothing to do with what kind of soup they have......After that the answer is followed, but only in Spanish and is not translated in the help language. There is a picture in the screen however, with some sort of vegetable soup, but the answer is \\"Hoy tenemos sopa de ajo casera\\" which I think is quite complicated to figure out that their answer is that they have soup (from the house or home made) with garlic!  This course is nice to learn vocabulary and to have on the side, but you do need a proper book or classes to get into the real conversational spanish, because just with this, it is not possible to learn all of that. I feel sorry for people who bought Rosetta Stone and spend so much money on this (since the reviews do acknowledge that it provides quite the same), because I do think that for this price, this is really a good product, they just should promise a bit less than they do now, and they should sell it as a great vocabulary builder, which it really is.

review_headline: Not Completely Backward Compatable or Featured
review_body: I have Magix Music Studio 12 and have made literally dozens of songs using its VIP format. I get Music Maker 16 and none of my VIP files can be used to work with it, so I have to make new versions of the songs using its new MMM or whatever format they use for song creation. The MIDI import function puts all of the MIDI tracks on one MMM track instead of giving you the option of having each MIDI track on its own MMM line; that ability is on Music Studio 12 Deluxe. I use 12 to separate the MIDI tracks into their own lines so that I can use the Vita feature to make each track more livelier; you can't do that with Music Maker 16.    Not on Amazon yet is Music Maker 16 Premium, which I would give three stars if it didn't have the same problem as the MM 16 basic. In Premium, there are even more Vita instruments, a new Beatbox, a new version of Revolta. The Atmos is lame with a mere four background sounds; why can't they upgrade it to have a wider selection like a nightclub bar, sports stadium crowd, and more.    Some features are improved, but what's needed is a patch to make Music Maker 16 work with the legacy VIP files, some of which use the synth tracks no longer seen on MM16 such as copper, silver, the original Beatbox, and whatever else I haven't discovered that's missing.    Also missing from each MMM line are direct volume and pan controls so you can control the sound without needing to dig deep into the menus to control them.    All in all, it falls short of being recommended to other people. Could've been better if it worked with its own legacy VIP file formats so we could easily improve on them and allowed us to split the imported MIDI tracks into their own separate MMM tracks.

review_headline: It's not Office 2007, and that's a good thing...
review_body:
... but it's similar - the difference being that it's the \\"growed-up\\" version of Office 2007. Much as Microsoft did with Windows 7 smoothing out the rough spots of Vista, so Win7 feels like (and is) a vastly improved new product, they did the same here with Office 2010. My first reaction to Offic 07 was not very positive - it looked cheapened and toy-like. Once 2010 installed, the first words out of my mouth were, \\"Ah, much better.\\" The elements of 2007 are all there - the much-loathed \\"ribbon\\" is ever present, but the candy-coating of colors has been subdued for something more adult and professional. If you got used to the odd, ever-changing world of \\"the ribbon\\" in 2007, you won't be surprised here, only pleased by it's mature new look.

The big difference in the suite, for me, is how Outlook now organizes the way Gmail does, in threaded conversation view, by grouping together all emails you've had with others in the same topic. This has been a great addition to Outlook that I use constantly in Gmail, making me rely more on Outlook than I have in the past.

Office 2010 behaves as well as it ever did, and has become a must-have in most people's day to day dealings with others on the internet. There are other options out there but each have their own failings that Office manages to best... other than price. Price alone is where Microsoft really sticks it to customers and it's hard to say it's truly \\"worth\\" the very high entry price for the full suite. Microsoft's made the unusual move of not allowing upgrades for this version, so users are forced into choosing one of three versions. Some can get away with the \\"home and student edition\\" but that lacks some pieces of the Office puzzle, most notably, to me, Outlook, which is available in the middle-of-the-road \\"home and business edition,\\" but is still quite pricey.

Is the upgrade worth it? It's hard to say. If your Office suite is in heavy use, most likely it will be a worthwhile upgrade. If not, as great as it is, users should probably pass, or wait until Microsoft comes to their senses and offers reasonable upgrade prices from older Office suites.t, as great as it is, users should probably pass, or wait until Microsoft comes to their senses and offers reasonable upgrade prices from older Office suites.

review_headline: As of 1.5, Quicken Essentials for Mac is Perfectly Fine
review_body: Most of the \\"most helpful\\" reviews here are of the initial release.  As of the latest 1.5 release, it works just fine, and for my money, it is still the best basic budgeting program out there that I've seen, and it runs on the Mac so I don't have to run VMWare Fusion every time I update my finances.    I used the basic features of the Windows version for years, and other than some differences in controls that took me about a week to get used to, this does everything I need it to do, and in its simplicity, it is better than the Windows one in some ways.    For example, 401Ks - I never could figure out how to tell Quicken that in one of my 401Ks I was 20% vested, but that 20% was never coming to me because I left the job.  In Quicken Essentials for Mac, it just grabs the balance for my 401K, broken out by investment - might not be what a power user wants, but I use this to store an overview of my financial picture and remind me to pay bills, not to manage every detail.  And I also had a different 401K in Windows where the managing institution sold all my shares in one managed set of securities and then gave me equivalent shares in another.  The sell never came through the online integration, causing it to get out of balance, and I never could figure out how to just enter a transaction to correct it.  Quicken for Windows kept trying to tell me that my correction to zero out the old investment was illegal short-selling and so couldn't be entered.  This was actually what drove me to go out and buy the Mac version.    The downloads also work better on Mac than they did on Windows (on Windows, even in 2010 version, I never did get some of my accounts working - they all work fine on Mac), and now that I am used to it, I like the interface for verifying downloaded transactions better in Mac than in Windows (I never let Quicken for Windows download transactions for the accounts I COULD get working because it forced you into a whole different clunky view to validate downloadedtransactions - in Quicken for Mac, you do it all in the main register for each account, and there is a separate column you can sort on to see just those things that have been downloaded that you haven't verified).    Overall, I'd say many of these reviews are negative about the initial release (which sounded like it was bad), or at least negative about lack of features I don't use, and so don't give credit for substantial improvements since, and for interface improvements on basic features.  It works better than the Windows one did for me.

Key among these is the persistency of the main-line, on-your-computer versions of these very familiar tools.  Sure, there are many web options, free options, etc., but for the true professional or student, this tightly integrated set of desktop tools still stands as a vital part of getting things done and done right.  Over the past few iterations, Microsoft has brought out a ribbon interface which, in this version has been extended out to maximize its potential.  As others have noted, the change from prior interfaces is not an easy one, but with an open mind and some dedicated time, I really think that my workflow has been maximized.  Undoubtably, Office can be complex - but in that complexity is power and the power to be creative and professional.  Candidly, some of my work is done on Mac and as much as I love the Mac, I cannot simply do everything I need to do with Apple's programs.  For example, Apple's Pages - a beautiful word processor in its own right - simply cannot format long footnotes - an absolute abomination for my work that has persisted over several iterations.  I'm happy to see the announcement that Office for Mac will be bringing the ribbon interface to Mac soon.  In the meantime, I recommend this product.

Having had such bad experiences with antivirus and other security programs in the past, I actually got to the point where I uninstalled all such programs from all 4 computers in my home network and have run without any protection for the past year now.  In the past I have used several older versions of Norton (including 2002 and others), and more recently Zone Alarm Security Suite, but found all of them to be more trouble than they were worth.  Generally they were like pouring glue into your computer, and caused no end of freeze ups, slow downs and thus complaints from family members.    I have now installed Norton Internet Security 2010 on several machines all running Windows 7 Pro, and have had (so far) a much more positive experience because once installed it doesn't seem to have any noticeable negative impacts.  I should also mention that installing it also had no POSITIVE impacts either - full system scans identified nothing worse on any of the previously-unprotected systems other than some tracking cookies.    The product name \\"Internet Security\\" well describes the product, because it goes WAY beyond just antivirus and antispam functionality in an attempt to protect you from virtually any badness that could conceivably enter your computer from outside.  Mostly this is good, but it does increase complexity in areas (see observations below).  The good news though is that this product does it in a way that is very automatic and inobtrusive.    Some observations and details:  - When I was ready to install the product, the first thing I did was go into Windows Control Panel/System/System Protection and set a restore point so I could roll back any changes in case Norton messed things up.  I have learned to do this before making any significant changes to any of my Windows machines, and I highly recommend this because the roll-back works very well if you need to do it.  - The installation process takes quite some time.  Once you insert the installation DVD to start the installation, the first thing it does is download 60 MB of data, which can take some time.  I suppose this was some kind of update.  - Once past that step, the rest of the installation process runs smoothly and automatically.  The only down side to this is that it makes a lot of decisions on its own.  Nothing that you can't undo, though.  - Like more and more software these days, this requires you to enter a lengthy product key and go through an \\"activation\\" process.  I find this annoying and objectionable, at least partly because I occasionally rebuild my computers and/or switch to a different main machine, and this wretched activation technology makes that very difficult.  Minus 1 star for this.  - As part of activation, it requires you to create an online account with Norton, another small annoyance.  On a positive note, it does not require you to enter a credit card number as some do so they can automatically renew your subscription.  However, it does tell you at bottom of its screen how many days are left on your subscription and provides a button labeled \\"Express Renewal\\" so you can renew.  Reminds me of what so many magazines do these days when you subscribe and then they start asking you if you'd like to renew even before you've gotten your first issue!  - It installs an extra control bar in both IE and Firefox to provide various security services.  This is one of the things it changes on your computer without asking.  This caused my wife an immediate problem so I had to tinker with it to get her going.  - It also creates a gadget on the desktop that tells you things are OK.      So far, so good, thus I am reasonably pleased at this point.  Hopefully this will continue to be the case in the long run.    Nothing to do with this product, but my experience of running more than a year with no additional security software does make me think that the best defense against bad stuff is ultimately well-educated users who are careful about what they click on. Thisproduct is a lot like a flu shot:  It's something that you would get if you are concerned that taking normal sanitary are not enough.  Most people will not get the flu regardless of whether they get a shot or not.  Even those who get the shot might still get the flu.  But if you are worried about the threat or feel particularly vulnerable, getting the shot will at least make you feel better.

Roxio Creator 2010 is a one stop, do-it-all software package meant to take care of all your media needs. Unfortunately, the product is a mixed bag.

I tried out Creator 2010 on my Vista desktop with 3GB RAM and Core 2 Duo processor. I see many angry reviewers say they had a hard time installing the package. The install worked for me, and took 15-20 minutes. I also have installed updates to the software. I've mostly gotten the software to work, but it can be slow and inconsistent at times.

You do get a lot of functionality in here if take the time to go through it all. The DVD/CD burning has lots of features. It's easy to do things like copy an unprotected double density DVD to a standard 4.7GB DVD (with compression) or just burn a collection of data files. It also has Blu-ray burning capabilities if you have a Blu-ray writer, which I do not and was unable to test. You can also have the software recognize your mp3 files and playlists and have it exported to your PSP or other mobile devices, but I only played around with that a little bit as it seemed like overkill and an unneeded feature for me.

The slideshow and movie editing options are pretty deep if you dig into them. There are lots of semi-pro looking transitions to choose from, and there is an easy to use visual bottom window that allows you to storyboard your pics or movie clips for playback. Adding music to your creations is seamless in the video editing section. It can all done on the storyboard, moving and shifting discrete elements as you wish. If you take a lot of videos or pictures and like to paste all your clips together, there is plenty for you to use here.

So what are the problems? Well, I didn't really have the same horrible experiences some other reviewers did. However, I did run into trouble when I would try to tie several movie clips together with transitions between the clips. Creator 2010 lets you stitch them together and export them as one continuous movie in a variety of different formats. But when I would choose to export to say, a regular .avi file, I would occasionally get a Preview window with an export status bar and absolutely nothing would happen. Sometimes it would work, sometimes it wouldn't. And even when it does work, it's not that fast. I couldn't figure out the basis of the inconsistency to save my life--I wasn't using other programs at the time, I didn't have any processes going in the background, nothing.

The other \\"problem\\" to consider is what do you want out of this software? Most computers have some kind of DVD burning software suite. Heck, even my desktop comes with a Lite version of Roxio burning software and that has always worked fine for me. Additionally, there are free programs out there that will compress video for you to fit it onto a 4.7GB DVD disc. Windows Movie Maker does many of things Creator 2010 does in terms of video editing, and that's also free to download. I admit Creator has more options when it comes to compressing and burning media, or adding transitions and music while editing video, but some of the software inconsistencies can drive you crazy.

Overall, I can't truly recommend Creator 2010. I can suggest it to you, though, under certain circumstances. If you have a Flip camera and want to just take clips of your kids on vacation and maybe stitch them together to burn a DVD to send to grandma, then you can get free software to do that for you. However, if you find Creator for a good price, and you want to try to edit movies with one extra level of polish compared to Windows Movie Maker, then this might work well enough for you. Also, if you have a new Blu-ray burner and want to edit and create HD movies on Blu-ray discs to give to people, then Creator really might be your ticket, but I wasn't able to try those features out. product_title: TELL ME MORE Arabic Complete Course
review_headline: Will cause problems for COMPLETE beginners
review_body: I majored in languages in college, including a lot of Spanish and was very pleased with TellMeMore's Spanish materials, so I bought this one to learn to read Arabic (and I've just started it).  U.S. Windows installations don't natively support Arabic.  The installation instructions only tell you how to install under Windows 2000, Windows 2003 (whatever that is supposed to be ...) and Windows XP.  No information at all on how to install under Vista or Win 7, not even on the website!  Available screen resolutions are 640x480, 800x600 and 1024x768, either 256 or 65k colors. The manual talks about video cards with ONE or TWO megabytes of RAM!    Regardless of your monitor's resolution, set it to 1024 or lower.    The \\"Help\\" is old Win 98 style and most of it is hype about how great the software is or ridiculous basics like, \\"you can adjust the volume and speed\\". Under \\"Options\\" => Options: Dialogue and Exercises => Dictation, the entire \\"help\\" entry:    Dictation    You can vary the difficulty level of the dictation. If you ask TeLL me More® to be lenient (easy mode), it will not grade any mistaken or forgotten punctuation marks. If, however, you want TeLL me More® to be more demanding (difficult mode), you will not be allowed to make any punctuation errors.     AND THAT'S ONE OF THE MOST DETAILED HELPS!    Once you \\"log in\\", the BACKGROUND will be a cartoon \\"film set\\".  Click on that. In the lower left are 3 books.  Cursor over those and the top will open with \\"Reference Tools\\".    Here's their explanation of the alphabet:    \\"There are twenty-eight letters in the Arabic alphabet. In most cases, the letters are connected to one another, their form varying slightly according to whether they are found at the beginning, middle or end of a word, or if they are isolated.     The following table lists all the letters in alphabetical order in each of the four positions: initial, medial, final and isolated.\\"    It would be nice if they spelled out the name of the letters inEnglish and said what sound each had -- but they don't.  Apparently they expect \\"Complete Beginners\\" to do a significant amount of research and study BEFORE starting!    I wound up returning this, for 2 reasons--the major one personal and not related to the TMM materials.  I didn't realize that, like Hebrew, ARABIC DOESN'T WRITE VOWELS. I know from having studied a little biblical Hebrew that unless you ALREADY KNOW the language WELL, it is EXTREMELY hard to read Semitic with only the consonants.  (Semitic words have a 3-consonant root and changing the vowels changes whether it is a noun, verb, etc.)    When I spoke with the TMM rep to return it I did also point out the lack of materials spelling out the name and pronunciation of each Arabic letter in English letters.  (I also had 5 semesters of Russian in college.)  His response was, \\"We use the immersion method.  You didn't learn English by starting with a book, you learned by listening, etc.    HUH??? WHERE DID HE GET THE RIDICULOUS IDEA THAT *ANYONE* LEARNS TO *READ* THEIR FIRST LANGUAGE BY \\"OSMOSIS\\"???    Introductory material for EVERY language I have studied have listed the alphabet and letters--French, German, Hebrew, Latin, Russian, Spanish and Yiddish.    HOWEVER, I did look through the materials overall and ASIDE FROM THE ALPHABET ISSUE they do look QUITE GOOD.  They do explain the various grammar principles, there is a lexicon (designated \\"Glossary\\"), etc.  From what I saw in both this and TMM's Spanish course they REALLY could improve their introductory \\"lay of the land\\" materials.  Pretty much everything you expect is there SOMEWHERE (except the Arabic alphabet list ...) but it is quite a challenge and quite annoying trying to FIND it.  And when you do, the first couple of times it will probably be by accident and you won't remember how you got there.

product_title: Jones in the Fast Lane, Cd Rom Software, By Sierra
review_body: \\"Jones\\" is an intriguing pastime, partly because YOU decide what wins.  Before the game begins, you are presented with a couple of areas: Money, Education, Happiness and Status.  You decide which one(s) will determine the winner. If you put all the Success points into Money, then you need to acquire a certain amount of wealth to win.  If you split the success points between Money and Status, you will need to acquire a fancy house and car in addition to a slightly smaller amount of earned income.  You can divide the points between all four in whatever ratio you like, give 0 points to Education or Happiness, etc.  It's all up to you.    Once you've decided what wins the game, you begin playing.  You start out as an unemployed high school graduate.  Each turn is one week.  You decide how to spend your time: looking for a job, going back to school, relaxing in your apartment, etc.  You can spend as much or as little on each of these as you want.  (Fortunately jobs are easy to obtain IF you have the necessary education and appropriate clothing.  The casual wear you purchased is fine for a fast food job, but no one will hire you for a sales or executive position.)  If you don't stop to eat or rest enough, eventually you get ill and can't work / go to school.  You get the idea.  It's a fairly realistic simulation of life after high school, but at the same time entertaining.    I came across this game a couple of years ago and installed it on our classroom computer.  In spite of the fact that the graphics were nowhere near \\"cutting edge,\\" my students enjoyed Jones a great deal.  Partly I suspect because THEY decided what would win, not the game.  Also, there's some sly humor in your interactions with the NPC's.      Since \\"Jones\\" didn't really fit into any existing game category, and doesn't seem to have had a large marketing push, it faded quickly from the marketplace (although I picked up a remaindered 10 year old copy for a few bucks at Office Depot).    Although the protagonist is a high school graduate, it's suitable for all ages.  IIRC there were one or two bits of mildly suggestive language that will most likely go over the head of younger children.  (One of the other reviewers gives the only example I can remember.)  I estimate the interest level would be for those 9 and up.  Think of it as the original \\"Oregon Trail\\" (I stopped after after the third edition, so I don't know what the later versions are like) but for contemporary life instead of pioneering.  Or try to imagine \\"The Sims\\" if it had come out 10 years earlier.    Although it's essentially a single player game, it's worth searching out as something the whole family will enjoy, particularly if you can pick it up inexpensively.

product_title: Intensive Course Tactics 1 Chess Middlegame Software
review_headline: Fair tactical problems, decent organization, bad interface
review_body:
I selected this product over its competitor, CT-Art, due to the number of tactical problems and price differential. I have used ChessBase programs in the past and have had good experiences with them, so I thought this would also be a good package. In some respects I was right, but in others, not so much.

Intensive Course Tactics (ICT) boasts over 4,000 tactical problems to work through and practice, which is very respectable. The sheer number of problems is enough to merit attention, but what is not clear is that a lot of these problems are very basic and suitable for beginners. Many, many problems in this collection are simple one- or two-move tactical finds, which are important even for more experienced players to know but they do not \\"feed\\" advanced players the kind of practice necessary to advance very far. Without question, less experienced players will glean the most knowledge from this collection. That's fine, but it should be made more clear in the packaging.

ICT is broken up into a multitude of databases which at first seems a little overwhelming, but the organization is actually reasonably good. There are databases for tactics relating to forks, windmills, pins, skewers, material capture and a whole lot more. There is naturally some overlap in theme but overall the organizational layout is logical.

The interface that is included with the ICT databases is not good. It is an old ChessBase reader and it is clunky, unattractive and a little awkward to use. The databases themselves are in ChessBass format though, so if you have a more recent version of Fritz/Hiarcs/Junior/etc., I would strongly encourage using that instead of the included reader to access the databases.

ICT is really not a bad product. It has a lot of good tactical training broken into very logical areas of practice, but mostly for players working their way up from the lower end of the class rankings. It is unfortunate that the reader with it is poor. While I can recommend this product for certain players, I would encourage stronger players to look at more challenging options.uct for certain players, I would encourage stronger players to look at more challenging options.

review_headline: Good basic functionality if you can get it to install
review_body: HR Block's tax apps have historically had problems installing and updating, especially on Macs. This year's version is worse than last year's.    1 I tried to install it on a Mac first. It refused to run properly, because the account I was using was not an admin account. I got it to run by switching to an admin account. This is the same behavior as it had shown last year and the year before that and the year before that, and was not a surprise. I'd reported the problem to the vendor last year, not really expecting them to change. They didn't. Memo to HR Block: It's good practice to _not_ use an admin account to run normal activities. Yes, Apple will let you set up an admin account to run normally. Yes, Microsoft will make it difficult to run under a standard account. And, yes, prudent security practice would be to _not use an admin account as the normal account_. And this goes double or triple for when you're running financial software... such as, well, tax software. I will be reporting the problem to HR Block again this year. I expect that they will continue to ignore me.    2 after it installed on the Mac I tried to update it. I have my personal Mac configured in two partitions, the Mac OS X partition (formatted HFS+ Journaled, as is standard) and a Boot Camp partition with Vista SP2 installed on a NTFS volume. I have several external drives connected to my Mac, by FireWire and USB, and I have some other items connected over my home network. The brain-damaged updater that HR Block uses insists on searching _each and every volume mounted on the filesystem_ before doing the update. This includes the NTFS partition, and the network volumes. It took literally four hours 37 minutes to search the NTFS partition. (I timed it.) This is actually slower than last year, when it only took three hours plus. (That's why I timed it this time...) I can unmount the external drives, I can unmount the network volumes, but I _can't_ unmount the Boot Camp partition... and no other installer wastes its time searching the Boot Camp partition for stuff that should only be found on the boot volume. Memo to HR Block: it might be a good idea to find a Mac update installer that isn't brain-dead. Doing something simple, such as ignoring NTFS partitions on the Mac side, or letting the customer uncheck volumes to be searched, might be a Good Idea.    3 I called HR Block's customer service while this was going on. They were clueless, same as last year. Two different CS reps didn't know that it was possible to install Windows on a Mac, either in a Boot Camp partition or using a VM. One tried to tell me that what I was doing was impossible. The other one seemed to be under the impression that I was installing the app on the Mac side so that I could use it on the Windows side. Memo to HR Block: training your CS staff on how Macs work would be a Good Idea.     4 while the updater was running on the Mac I dug out my Windows laptop and installed the app there. I then updated it, and despite the fact that the laptop was connected to the same network volumes (and to the Mac!) the updater ran quickly and confined its search to logical places. This was a Good Thing, as it turns out...    5 the app found the copy of my last year's return that I'd copied over to the laptop and loaded it and got me started on my return. I was able to finish my return before the updater on the Mac was finished. (Memo to HR Block: you've really got to do something about that updater...) and that's when I found out that apparently when it found that copy of my last year's return, it loaded it up into the new return... and _then deleted the old one_. I needed something from the old one which wasn't available in the new one, and I couldn't find the old one anywhere on my system. I'd put my last four year's returns into a folder named 'Taxes' on my Mac, and had copied that folder over to the laptop. The folder was still there, the return for the year before last and the two years before thatwere still there... but last year's return was gone. Missing. History. Fortunately I still had it on the Mac, so I copied it over again, ran last year's HR Block app (which tried to update despite being a year old) got the required info and entered it into the new return. If I hadn't had multiple copies of my stuff spread over several machines I'd have been in big trouble. (Well, I'd have had to actually dig up the paper version and type stuff in, but the whole point behind having electronic records is so I don't have to do that...) Memo to HR Block: maybe it would be a Good Idea to _not delete the old return_?    Now, once I got it to behave it worked. It's just that I shouldn't have had to go to all this trouble to get it to work.

product_title: Fluenz Spanish (Latin America) 1 for Mac, PC, iPhone, iPad & Android Phones, Version 3
review_body: Fluenz is like a real classroom with an on-screen teacher who is a native Spanish speaker. Although I think there is room for improvement in the usability of the Fluenz interface, I have found that the Fluenz approach works for me and is helping me learn. I bought all five levels and I'm currently half way through Spanish 2.    Each Fluenz session starts with a short intro letting you know what you're about to learn. Next you listen to a dialogue three times, with and without English and Spanish subtitles. The instructor then spends six to ten minutes explaining the grammatical structures, verb conjugations, and new vocabulary. Exercises follow, in which you will type what you hear, match what you hear to images, match Spanish and English phrases, repeat the pronunciation, and record your own dialogue. The exercises are generally well constructed and build up slowly the way a good teacher would cover the material in a class.    The dialogues are focused on real-world situations that you could be expected to find yourself in as a visitor to a Spanish-speaking country. For example, you'll learn the words to speak about going to a hotel, buying a cellphone, taking a taxi, and asking how much something costs. Fluenz does not try to teach you the broadest vocabulary or every grammatical structure.    Fluenz requires a lot of typing, so you may find Fluenz more challenging than competing products if you're not a touch typist. Fortunately, you can ignore accents if you choose. Typing is important even if you will never write in Spanish because it's easy to recognize the best option in a list of choices, but it's more difficult to stare at a blank screen and have the words come to mind. Typing requires that you be more fully engaged so you are learning more actively.    Fluenz's interface is attractive and is entirely Flash based. There are several small usability problems and a couple of Mac-only challenges. These issues will not stop you from learning Spanish, but the usability could be improved.
